rewritten:
The legislative branch of the Associated Students was the Student Congress, called Congress in the document that created it. The constitution printed in the College Heights Herald on 7 April 1966 vested the legislative authority of the Associated Students in Congress and set out its composition. Each of the four class councils sent its president, its vice president and one representative at large, twelve seats in all. Professional and honor groups, departmental clubs and general clubs sent one representative each. The Interfraternity Council, the Panhellenic Council, the men's residence halls and the women's residence halls sent two apiece. Two representatives were elected at large. That came to twenty-five seats. The four officers of the Associated Students served as officers of Congress and sat in it as well: the vice president, secretary and treasurer as voting members, and the president presiding, voting only to break a tie, and required to give the secretary an agenda ten days before a meeting. Officers and members took office in the second week of May and served one calendar year. Two-thirds of the total membership had to be present before Congress could consider business.

Congress gave final approval to the budget, which the Finance Committee prepared and the Executive Council approved in draft, approved constitutional appointments, and ruled on petitions from student organizations seeking University recognition, Greek-letter social fraternities excepted. It could delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods by a three-fourths vote, remove a member for just cause by a three-fourths vote on secret ballot, set its bylaws by two-thirds, and amend the constitution by two-thirds of its full membership followed by a majority of students voting in a regular election. Every change was subject to University approval. Three constitutional committees answered to it: Rules and Elections, Finance, and Student Activities, five members each, at least two of them seniors.

The roster of the first Congress kept by the President's Office lists twenty-five people. Four are the officers, so twenty-one of the twenty-five seats are accounted for: two Interfraternity and two Panhellenic representatives, two men's residence hall representatives and one woman's, one each for professional and honorary fraternities, departmental clubs and general college clubs, two campus-wide representatives at large, and three seats each for the senior, junior and sophomore classes. No freshman seat appears, and the archive does not say why. Three of the twenty-five, David Arvin, Forrest (Bucky) Lanning and Marshall Peace, are marked as members of the Executive Council, matching the three representatives the constitution had Congress elect from its own number. TopSCHOLAR's description of the roster dates the election of these officers to May 1966.

The apportionment was challenged early. The Herald reported on 20 February 1969 that Congress had voted 18 to 1 the previous week for Kent Gildersleeve's resolution to form a revision committee, and had elected Gildersleeve, junior class representative Mike Durham and sophomore class vice-president Doug Alexander to it. Gildersleeve, who held the general clubs seat, said clubs and professional and service fraternities with memberships as large as Greek organizations had no direct representative while the Panhellenic and Interfraternity Councils had two each. President Bill Straeffer backed the resolution, called the existing constitution barely adequate and said one representative stood for about forty clubs. Sophomore class president Steve Stephens cast the only vote against, saying the question had been brought up hurriedly and that members had not been told what needed changing. Straeffer was to appoint two further members, one from the Judicial Council and one from the Executive Council, the chairman of Congress could appoint more subject to Congress's approval, and the committee was capped at ten and due to report on 8 May 1969.

The Herald of 24 April 1970 reported that Congress had instead read and approved four constitutional changes at a recent session, the date of which the paper does not give. They were a change in membership and voting rights covering the right of graduate students to hold elected office, approved in a form requiring a candidate to be an undergraduate and to stay one throughout the term; the addition of two members from each of the colleges together with two more representatives at large; the establishment of inferior judicial councils; and impeachment of members of Congress. All four were to go to students on the campus cheerleader election ticket the following month. At the same session Steve Todd of the constitutional revision committee urged Congress to consider an at-large system of representation in place of the guaranteed seat system then in use, and parliamentarian Phil Meyers concurred, arguing that Greeks, dormitories and clubs did not represent the student body and that groups such as black students and veterans had little voice under it.

The earliest numbered piece of Congress legislation the archive holds for these years is Associated Students Congress Bill No. 3, the Environmental Commission, written by vice president David Porter and passed in a regular session on 14 May 1970. It created a nine-member commission of five students, two faculty and two administrators to alert university, city, state and federal agencies to problems of pollution, environment and health, and to report annually to Congress. Porter circulated the bill to faculty and administrators the next day.
problems:
Six problems, three of them of the kind the checklist names.

1. A publication date read as an event date. "On 24 April 1970 Congress read and approved four amendments" puts the vote on the Friday the Herald came out. Paul Hightower's article gives no date for the session, says only that it happened "during a lengthy session", refers back to "last week's meeting" and forward to business to be voted on "at next week's meeting". Structure fact 23 carries the same error.

2. Two dates no structure fact carries, one of them a bare headline. "A proposed new constitution went back for study in November 1969 and work on it halted in January 1970" rests on nothing in the structure array. The January claim traces to the index line "Work Halts on Constitution" in Herald 49:24, 13 Jan 1970, an untouched headline. This repository's own rule is that a headline is not the article beneath it. Both sentences should stay out until someone reads the two issues; the November item is in years.json but cited to an index entry whose text is truncated.

3. An invented reason. "no freshman seats appear, those being filled in the fall" states a cause. The roster shows the absence; no source in this block says why. The constitution in fact says all members took office in the second week of May, and only exempts freshman class representatives from the one-semester attendance rule, which is suggestive but not a record of practice.

4. A count that misleads. "enumerated twenty-five seats" followed by "The roster ... lists twenty-five people" reads as a full house. It was not. The roster's twenty-five are the four officers plus twenty-one seat-holders; three freshman seats and one of the two women's residence hall seats are unfilled. The officers were themselves members of Congress under Article II, so the body's total membership was larger than the twenty-five seats of Article III Section 4, which matters because quorum was two-thirds of total membership.

5. A ratification date the facts do not carry and the archive puts in doubt. "The constitution students ratified in April 1966" appears in no structure fact. The Herald index has 45:21 of 28 April 1966 still headlining that the constitution "Shoots for Ratification Vote" and 45:22 of 5 May 1966 reporting "Charter Passes Easily", which points past April. The month should go until someone reads those two issues. Likewise "The first Congress was elected in May 1966" comes from TopSCHOLAR's catalogue description of the roster, not from the roster or from any structure fact, and should be attributed.

6. Two small over-readings. "Three constitutional committees stood under it" overstates Congress's ownership: under Article V the committees act as directed by Congress or the Executive Council, and their members are recommended by the president with Executive Council approval. And "The apportionment was attacked early" is a shade stronger than the record, which shows a resolution carried 18 to 1 with its author and the president both speaking for it.

Everything else in the summary is sound, including the seat breakdown, the officers' voting rights, the quorum, the term of office, the Finance Committee budget route (Article V Section 6.a and Article VIII Section 1 both confirm it), the delegation, removal, bylaw and amendment thresholds, and every quoted position in the February 1969 dispute: Gildersleeve on clubs and service fraternities, Straeffer on one representative for about forty clubs, and Stephens as the lone vote against calling the question hurried. All three check out against the article.

verdicts.claim: The constitution made the legislative branch the Student Congress, referred to throughout the text as Congress, and gave it the legislative authority of the Associated Students (Article III, Sections 1 and 3).
verdicts.note: Read the constitution PDF (TopSCHOLAR sga article 1000, printed as Herald p.8, 7 Apr 1966). Article III Section 1: the legislative branch shall be the Student Congress, hereinafter called Congress. Section 3: Congress shall have all legislative authority of the Associated Students. Cite is exact.

verdicts.claim: Article III, Section 4 enumerated twenty-five Congress seats: Senior, Junior, Sophomore and Freshman Councils, three each (president, vice president, one representative at large); Professional and Honor groups one; Departmental Clubs one; General Clubs one; Interfraternity Council two; Panhellenic Council two; residence halls (men) two; residence halls (women) two; at-large representatives two.
verdicts.note: Section 4 lists exactly these units and numbers. The figure twenty-five is the researcher's arithmetic, not a number the section states, but the sum is right (12+3+2+2+2+2+2). Note for the summary's benefit: the four officers were also members of Congress under Article II, so total membership exceeded twenty-five.

verdicts.claim: Article III, Section 2 provided that the officers of the Associated Students served as the officers of Congress. The president, vice president, secretary and treasurer were elected by the student body in campus-wide elections (Article II, Section 1).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 2 and Article II Section 1 read as claimed, close to verbatim.

verdicts.claim: The vice president, the secretary and the treasurer were each made voting members of Congress. The president was a non-voting member except to resolve a tie, presided over all meetings of Congress and the Executive Council, and had to submit an agenda to the secretary at least ten days before a meeting of Congress.
verdicts.note: Article II Section 2.b.4, 2.b.8 and 2.b.9 (president); Section 3.b.6, 4.b.6 and 5.b.6 (vice president, secretary, treasurer each a voting member of Congress). The ten-day agenda duty is 2.b.9, in consultation with the Executive Council.

verdicts.claim: Quorum: Congress had to have present two-thirds of its total membership for consideration of business (Article III, Section 7c).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 7.c reads: have present two-thirds of its total membership for consideration of business. Citation letter is correct.

verdicts.claim: Term of office: the president, vice president, secretary and treasurer and all members of Congress assumed the duties of office during the second week of May and served for one calendar year (Article IX).
verdicts.note: Article IX, Term of Office, reads as claimed, close to verbatim.

verdicts.claim: Qualifications for a Congress representative: enrolled full-time undergraduate; in good standing with the University; 2.0 academic standing or higher; and, except freshman class representatives, in attendance one semester immediately preceding candidacy. Upper-class representatives needed minimum semester hours including current load: sophomore 25, junior 55, senior 85 (Article III, Section 5).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 5.a-e. The hour thresholds are stated as minimum semester hours including current academic load: Sophomore 25, Junior 55, Senior 85. All five items check out.

verdicts.claim: Vacancies in Congress were filled by the electoral unit whose congressional seat was vacant, in a manner acceptable to the Rules and Elections Committee (Article III, Section 6). All other vacancies were filled by presidential appointment subject to approval of Congress (Article X).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 6 and Article X both read as claimed. Section 6 opens with 'except as otherwise specified in this constitution', which the claim leaves out but which the second sentence effectively covers.

verdicts.claim: Powers of Congress under Article III, Section 7b: hear and give final approval of the budget; approve constitutional appointments; extend the jurisdiction and activities of the constitutional committees when necessary; and function as a judicial body in impeachment proceedings.
verdicts.note: Article III Section 7.b items 1-4, in the same order and almost the same words.

verdicts.claim: Congress ruled on petitions from student organizations seeking University recognition, except Greek-letter social fraternities, which were subject to the governing powers granted to the Interfraternity and Panhellenic Councils by the University. A two-thirds affirmative vote recommended the petitioning group for recognition (Article III, Section 7e).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 7.e, including the two-thirds affirmative vote and the Greek-letter exception. Citation letter correct.

verdicts.claim: Congress could delegate executive power to the Executive Council for fixed periods of time and within prescribed areas of authority by a three-fourths vote (Article III, Section 7d).
verdicts.note: Article III Section 7.d, near verbatim.

verdicts.claim: Impeachment and recall (Article XI): a member of Congress could be removed for just cause by a three-fourths vote of Congress acting as a judicial body, voting by secret ballot. Proceedings required the endorsement of at least five members of Congress, and a final vote could not be called until at least ten days after proceedings were instituted. An expelled representative could be re-admitted on petition and a three-fourths vote.
verdicts.note: Article XI, Impeachment and Recall. Every element including the five endorsements and the ten-day interval is in the text.

verdicts.claim: Three constitutional committees were created: Rules and Elections, Finance and Student Activities. Each carried five members, at least two of them seniors during their term, with the same qualifications as members of Congress; each chairman called and presided over committee meetings and reported to Congress (Article V).
verdicts.note: Article V Section 1 (the three committees), Section 2.a (five members, at least two seniors), Section 2.b (same qualifications as members of Congress) and Section 4 (chairman calls and presides, reports to Congress).

verdicts.claim: The Executive Council consisted of the president, vice president, secretary and treasurer plus three representatives elected by and from Congress. It carried out policies established by Congress, gave preliminary approval to the budget subject to action of Congress, and processed applications for recognition from student organizations (Article II, Section 6).
verdicts.note: Article II Section 6 and its items a.1, a.3 and a.4. The constitution's recognition clause excepts Greek letter social fraternities, which this claim omits, but structure fact 10 records the exception, so nothing is lost across the block.

verdicts.claim: Congress established its bylaws by a two-thirds vote, and amendments reported out of the Rules and Elections Committee also required two-thirds. All election laws and regulations had to be in the bylaws (Article XII).
verdicts.note: Article XII, Bylaws, near verbatim.

verdicts.claim: Amendment procedure (Article XIII): a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress followed by ratification in a regular election by a majority of the student body voting. All changes in the constitution were subject to approval by the University. Article XIV made the constitution effective when approved by the University and ratified by a majority of the student body voting.
verdicts.note: Articles XIII and XIV, near verbatim.

verdicts.claim: A Student Affairs Board sat outside the three branches: the Dean of Students as chairman, the Assistant Dean of Students, the Dean of Women, two faculty appointed by the President of the University, the president and vice president of Associated Students, the chairman of the Judicial Council, and one member appointed by and from the Executive Council. It ruled on directives or legislation issued by the branches or committees when these entered areas not specified in the constitution.
verdicts.fixed: A Student Affairs Board sat outside the three branches, nine members with equal voice and vote: the Dean of Students as chairman, the Assistant Dean of Students, the Dean of Women, two faculty appointed by the President of the University, the president and vice president of Associated Students, the chairman of the Judicial Council, and one member appointed by and from the Executive Council. It ruled on directives or legislation issued by the branches or committees when these entered areas not specified in the constitution nor authorized by the University, and its decisions were binding on all parties. It considered only matters referred to it by the president of Associated Students, the Dean of Students or the President of the University (Article VI).
verdicts.note: Membership list is exactly right, and Article VI is the right article (Article IV is the Judicial Council, Article V the committees). But the ruling power is over-stated by one word: Article VI Section 3 requires the matter to enter areas 'not specified in the constitution nor authorized by the University', two conditions, not one. Article VI Section 4 also limits the Board to matters referred to it, which the claim does not mention.

verdicts.claim: Each class elected a president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer and a congressman. The 2 May 1968 results list all five posts for the senior, junior and sophomore classes; the congressman elected was the class representative at large who sat in Congress.
verdicts.fixed: The 2 May 1968 results memo lists five posts for each of the senior, junior and sophomore classes: president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer and congressman. verdicts.claim: The spring 1968 ballot carried a constitutional amendment to revise the qualifications for treasurer, alongside cheerleader and student fee questions.
verdicts.note: Read the ballot PDF (dlsc_ua_records/528). It carries three items: vote for six varsity cheerleaders; a student assessment resolution asking the President and Board of Regents to raise registration fees by $1.50 a semester, the money allocated to Associated Students for low-cost entertainment; and a treasurer amendment adding a qualification that the treasurer be an accounting or business major or minor with at least six credit hours of accounting.

verdicts.claim: Acting on Kent Gildersleeve's resolution, Congress elected Mike Durham (junior class representative), Doug Alexander (sophomore class vice-president) and Gildersleeve to the constitution revision committee. Two further members, one from the Judicial Council and one from the Executive Council, were to be appointed by president Bill Straeffer, and the chairman of Congress could make further appointments subject to approval of Congress on condition the committee not exceed ten members. The committee was to submit its final revision to Congress on 8 May 1969.
verdicts.note: Read Bruce Tucker's article on page 1 of Herald 48:18, 20 Feb 1969. Every element is there, including the three elected members with those exact descriptions, the two Straeffer appointees from the Judicial and Executive Councils, the chairman's further appointments subject to Congress and the ten-member cap, and the 8 May deadline. The article also fixes the vote as 18 to one 'last week', so the summary's 'the previous week' is right.

The four were: a change in membership and voting rights covering the right of graduate students to hold elected office, approved in a form requiring anyone running for office to be an undergraduate and to remain so throughout the tenure of office; the addition of two members from each of the colleges together with two more representatives at large; the establishment of inferior judicial councils; and impeachment of members of Congress. verdicts.note: Same article. Todd is described as a member of the constitutional revision committee and suggested an at-large system rather than the guaranteed seat system 'which is used now'; the continuation on page 8 has parliamentarian Phil Meyers concurring and arguing that Greeks, dorms and clubs were not representative of the student body.

verdicts.claim: Associated Student Congress Bill No. 3 established an Environmental Commission. Vice president David Porter circulated it to WKU faculty with a memo dated 15 May 1970, the bill attached. It is the earliest numbered piece of Congress legislation the archive holds for this era; data/legislation.json indexes nothing earlier than 1991-92.
verdicts.note: Read dlsc_ua_records/568. The attached bill creates a nine-member Environmental Commission (five students, two faculty, two administrators) with the vice president as a standing member; Porter's covering memo of 15 May 1970 says the bill passed in a regular session of Congress the previous afternoon, i.e. 14 May 1970. The memo went to faculty members and administrators, not faculty alone, a small under-statement rather than an over-claim. I confirmed data/legislation.json: 390 entries, earliest session 1991-92; and a scan of data/herald-index-full.json for 1966-1971 returns no other numbered Congress bill. Porter was also the bill's author, which the block does not claim.

rewritten:
The legislative body of the Associated Students was its Congress. Its regular meeting was on Tuesday, and where the SGA records give a start time it is 5 p.m. For 1986-87 through spring 1992 the collection holds 135 sets of minutes and agendas. Of these, 127 are the Bowling Green body rather than the Glasgow campus, and 125 of those carry a Tuesday date; the two exceptions are 28 November 1988 and 27 October 1990. Survival is uneven by session: 25 sets for 1986-87, 6 for 1987-88, 24 for 1988-89, 36 for 1989-90 (28 of them Bowling Green), 28 for 1990-91 and 16 for 1991-92. All six surviving 1987-88 sets record a 5 p.m. start, and 68 sets across the block do.

Congress worked through bills and resolutions, numbered in separate series that restarted each semester and carried an F or S suffix. The two series could carry the same number in one term: spring 1991 produced both Bill #91-7-S, on presidential scholar recognition, and Resolution 91-7-S, on an intramural field. The surviving originals held in this repository were printed on Associated Student Government letterhead with a status block for first reading, second reading, pass, fail and other, a purpose line, whereas clauses and a therefore clause. Author and sponsor lines appear but not on every measure and not always both. On Resolution 91-2-F a standing committee, Student Affairs, occupies the author line and there is no sponsor line; on Resolution 91-6-F a named member is the sponsor and there is no author line. Bill #91-6-S, in spring 1991, was a by-law bill on overriding vetoes. The Herald of 14 March 1991 reported that a resolution on emergency road kits had survived a veto; the article itself was not read, so the date of the vote and the size of the majority are not known.

Members were elected with the executive each April, and further congress and freshman seats were filled in fall elections. Seats were also filled by a vote of Congress at a meeting: the Herald of 4 February 1988 reported four positions filled that way. In the issue of 22 March 1988 the Herald reported that 2 of 32 Associated Student Government positions were contested; the figure covers ASG positions generally and not congress seats alone.

Seats fell vacant. The Herald of 22 October 1987 reported that a member, Nick Hicks, had lost his seat, and the issue of 27 October reported that the body would get tough on absenteeism; no source found gives the reason for the Hicks seat loss, and the two items should not be read as one. The Herald of 23 February 1988 reported that ASG had set out its reasons for its vacancies. The Herald of 29 March 1990 reported that Congress had voted to expand itself, a week after reporting that it might add representatives. No source found records the seat count that resulted, or whether the expansion was carried out.

A consolidated text, the Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments, is dated 4 August 1986 and sits in the SGA records alongside an earlier unamended constitution of the Associated Students. Its contents were not read for this block, so how it apportioned seats, and what quorum it set, are not established here. Amendments went to the students: the Herald of 12 November 1987 reported that 81 students had voted to approve a set, and the issue of 9 April 1987 reported an amendment defeated for want of members present. A Judicial Council sat alongside Congress; its membership roster for 1986-87 survives, dated August 1986. The Herald of 17 January 1991 reported that two ASG officers, Amos Gott and Van Hodge, had stepped down; the headline gives neither their offices nor their reasons. The minutes of 15 March 1988 carry a description of awards naming the Dero Downing Award, Outstanding Congress Member, Outstanding Committee Member, the Dean Charles A. Keown Award, the Kerrie Faye Stewart Memorial Award and the Mary Angela Norcia Award.

Bill #92-10-S, introduced 1 April 1992, was a bill to change Associated Student Government to Student Government Association by constitutional amendment. The university's own history page records that the Associated Students voted on 7 April 1992, that a student referendum approved the change on 14 April, and that it took effect in fall 1992. No source found gives the turnout for that referendum. By 17 November 1992 the renamed body had a four-college representative structure: Bill #92-13-F of that date proposed the appointment of the required alternates.
problems:
The summary fails on five of the six listed triggers and cannot go out under the university's name as written.

NUMBERS THE FACTS DO NOT CARRY. (a) The minutes counts are wrong and internally inconsistent. The summary says 133 sets survive, then lists per-session figures that add to 131. The TopSCHOLAR Minutes listing (https://digitalcommons.wku.edu/sga/Meetings/Minutes/, single page, no pagination, 843 items) gives 135 items dated July 1986 to June 1992: 25 (1986-87), 6 (1987-88), 24 (1988-89), 36 (1989-90), 28 (1990-91), 16 (1991-92). Two of the six per-session figures are wrong. (b) "of the 124 that are neither Glasgow-campus nor executive-council records, 122 are dated on a Tuesday": there are ZERO executive-council records in this range, the non-Glasgow total is 127, and 125 of those carry a Tuesday date. (c) "Two 1987-88 sets record a 5 p.m. start" is wrong twice: the block's own structure fact names four, and the listing shows all six surviving 1987-88 sets at 5:00 PM (Minutes 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64), as do 68 sets across the block. (d) "students ratified on 14 April with about 1,200 voting" invents a referendum turnout. The WKU SGA history page, the only source cited for the referendum, gives no figure. The ~1,200 in this archive belongs to the presidential election reported in Herald 67:53, 16 Apr 1992 ("Joe Rains wins big as 1,200 turn out", years.json 1991-92), not to the rename ballot.

CLAIMS NO STRUCTURE FACT CARRIES. The committee list ("Student Affairs, Public Relations, Legislative Research, Academic Affairs and Campus Improvements") rests on no fact in the structure; only Student Affairs is evidenced, on the author line of Resolution 91-2-F. "Most output was a request to a named administrator, sent out as correspondence over the president's signature" rests on nothing at all. The whole impeachment sentence, and four of the five vacancy items (a class president quitting in January 1988, reasons given 23 February 1988, half the open slots filled in November 1988, vacancies on the agenda in March 1992, a February 1992 bill adding three non-traditional seats), appear in no structure fact. I found no such February 1992 bill in the SGA Legislation Bills listing.

CONTINUITY WITHOUT RECORD. "Vacancies ran through the whole period" asserts a thread across six sessions from scattered items, four of them unsourced. The archive has no vacancy record at all for 1986-87, 1988-89 or 1990-91.

HEADLINES READ AS ARTICLES, AND ISSUE DATES READ AS EVENT DATES. Six dates in the summary are Herald publication dates presented as the day the thing happened: the 14 March 1991 override, the 12 November 1987 ratification, the 9 April 1987 failed amendment, the 29 March 1990 expansion vote, the 19 November 1987 impeachment and the 3 December drop. Each event necessarily preceded its issue. Worse, "The override was used on 14 March 1991" states a procedural act that the headline (Herald 66:49, "Emergency Kit Resolution Survives Veto") does not describe; the article was not read. The watchdog committee is the 10 December 1987 issue, not 3 December, so that sentence merges two issues into one date.

A CHAIR TREATED AS AN OFFICER, A SPONSOR MISTAKEN FOR AN AUTHOR. "closed with author and sponsor lines; the sponsor was usually a standing committee" is backwards on the only originals we hold. In data/legislation/1991-92/resolution_91-2-f.pdf the standing committee (Student Affairs) is on the AUTHOR line and there is no sponsor line; in resolution_91-6-f.pdf a named member (Mistianna Holcomb) is the SPONSOR and there is no author line; resolution_92-7-s.pdf and bill_92-01-s.pdf carry neither. Separately, structure fact 17 turns a Judicial Council chairmanship into an ASG office in order to hang a constitutional eligibility rule on it, and neither the role nor the rule is in the cited headline.

MISCELLANEOUS. "Tuesday evenings" overstates a 5 p.m. start. "2 of 32 congress positions" changes the source, which says Associated Student Government positions, a wider set that includes the executive. "Twenty years of amendments were consolidated into one document" is read off a title; the researcher states plainly he could not open the PDF.

verdicts.claim: The legislative body was called Congress. Herald headlines of the period name it directly: bills passed "Congress," one member wrote most of "Congress bills," congress positions were filled at meetings, and the body voted to expand "Congress."
verdicts.note: All four headline strands check out. Herald 62:46, 19 Mar 1987 (dlsc_ua_records/5918) carries "Martin Luther King Bill Passes Congress Members Split by Argument", confirmed on the TopSCHOLAR landing page. The other three are corroborated elsewhere: Herald 63:37, 4 Feb 1988 (7471) "4 Student Government Association Congress Positions Filled at Meeting"; Herald 65:49, 29 Mar 1990 (7629) "Associated Student Government Votes to Expand Congress"; and the one-member-wrote-most-of-the-bills item at Herald 62:29, 11 Dec 1986 (5825), already in data/years.json. The fact bundles four sources under one citation label, which an editor may want to split, but nothing in it is wrong.

verdicts.claim: Congress met weekly on Tuesdays. 133 sets of minutes and agendas survive across the six sessions; of the 124 that are neither Glasgow-campus nor executive-council records, 122 carry a Tuesday date. Per session the surviving count is 25 (1986-87), 6 (1987-88), 24 (1988-89), 36 (1989-90), 25 (1990-91) and 15 (1991-92).
verdicts.note: The Tuesday cadence is real, but almost every number is wrong. I parsed the full TopSCHOLAR Minutes listing (843 items, one page, no pagination). For July 1986 to June 1992 it holds 135 items, not 133. Per session: 25, 6, 24, 36, 28, 16 - so 1990-91 and 1991-92 are both understated. There are ZERO executive-council records in this range, so that exclusion category is fictitious; the eight excluded items are all Glasgow. The non-Glasgow total is 127, of which 125 are Tuesday and two are not (Monday 28 Nov 1988, Saturday 27 Oct 1990). The block's own summary compounds this: 25+6+24+36+25+15 = 131, not the 133 it states.
verdicts.fixed: Congress met on Tuesdays. 135 sets of minutes and agendas survive across the six sessions; of the 127 that are not Glasgow-campus records, 125 carry a Tuesday date, the exceptions being 28 November 1988 and 27 October 1990. Per session the surviving count is 25 (1986-87), 6 (1987-88), 24 (1988-89), 36 (1989-90, of which 28 are the Bowling Green body), 28 (1990-91) and 16 (1991-92). The collection holds no executive-council minutes for these years.

verdicts.claim: Meetings were held at 5 p.m.: the minutes of 17 November 1987, 1 March 1988, 15 March 1988 and 19 April 1988 all carry a 5:00 PM start time in the collection's own metadata.
verdicts.note: Confirmed item by item on the Minutes listing and on the individual landing pages. Minutes/62 (17 Nov 1987) reads 5:00 PM to 5:50 PM; Minutes/61 (1 Mar 1988) 5:00 PM to 5:50 PM; Minutes/60 (15 Mar 1988) 5:00 PM to 6:20 PM; Minutes/59 (19 Apr 1988) 5:00 PM to 6:40 PM. Worth telling the editor that this undercounts: the remaining two 1987-88 sets (Minutes/63 and /64) also carry 5:00 PM, so all six do, as do all 24 of 1988-89, 15 of 1986-87 and 17 of 1989-90 - 68 across the block. 1990-91 and 1991-92 record no time at all. The summary's "Two 1987-88 sets" is flatly wrong against this fact and against the source.

verdicts.claim: Legislation came in two instruments, bills and resolutions, numbered in separate series that restarted each semester and carried an F (fall) or S (spring) suffix. The two series could carry the same number in the same term: spring 1991 produced both a Bill #91-7-S and a Resolution 91-7-S on different subjects.
verdicts.note: The Bills and Resolutions listings on TopSCHOLAR bear this out. Each F and S run restarts at 1. The collision is exact: Bill #91-7-S is "Presidential Scholar Recognition" (Bills/133) and Resolution 91-7-S is "Intramural Field" (Resolutions/174), two different subjects in spring 1991. The four originals in data/legislation/1991-92/ confirm the suffix convention is the calendar year of the semester: Resolution 91-2-F and 91-6-F are dated in autumn 1991, Bill 92-01-S 28 January 1992, Resolution 92-07-S 2 April 1992.

verdicts.claim: Every measure was printed on Associated Student Government letterhead with a status block for First Reading, Second Reading, Pass, Fail and Other, a PURPOSE line, WHEREAS clauses, a THEREFORE clause, and separate AUTHOR and SPONSOR lines. Four such originals from 1991-92 are held in this repository at data/legislation/1991-92/.
verdicts.note: I extracted the text of all four PDFs in data/legislation/1991-92/ (all verified as real PDFs). The count of four is right and the letterhead, status block, PURPOSE, WHEREAS and THEREFORE elements are on three of them. But "Every measure" and "separate AUTHOR and SPONSOR lines" both fail, and they fail on the very document the fact cites as its exemplar. resolution_91-6-f.pdf shows no letterhead, a differently laid out status block with no Other, and a Sponsor line naming a member with no Author line. resolution_91-2-f.pdf carries an Author line reading Student Affairs and no Sponsor line. resolution_92-7-s.pdf and bill_92-01-s.pdf carry neither. This is the error that produced the reversed claim in the summary that the sponsor was usually a standing committee: on this evidence the committee sits on the author line and the individual on the sponsor line.
verdicts.fixed: The surviving originals were printed on Associated Student Government letterhead with a status block for First Reading, Second Reading, Pass, Fail and Other, a PURPOSE line, WHEREAS clauses and a THEREFORE clause. Author and sponsor lines appear but not on every measure and not always both: of the four originals held in this repository at data/legislation/1991-92/, Resolution 91-2-F carries a standing committee on its author line and no sponsor, Resolution 91-6-F carries a named member as sponsor and no author, and the other two carry neither. Resolution 91-6-F is also laid out differently and shows no letterhead.

verdicts.claim: Legislation required two readings before a vote. The Herald reported the recycling resolution having its first reading on 19 September 1991, a week before the body acted on it.
verdicts.note: The headline is exact: Herald 67:7, 19 Sep 1991 (dlsc_ua_records/7775) carries "Associated Student Government Has First Reading On Recycling Resolution", confirmed on the landing page. Two over-claims. First, 19 September 1991 is the issue date, so the first reading happened in the days before it, not on it. Second, "a week before the body acted on it" has no source: I checked the following two issues, 67:8 of 24 September (7774) and 67:9 of 26 September (7773), and neither indexes any follow-up on the recycling resolution. The general two-readings rule is a fair inference from the status blocks on the surviving originals, but the cited headline does not state a requirement.
verdicts.fixed: The printed status block on surviving measures provides for a first and a second reading. The Herald of 19 September 1991 reported that a recycling resolution had had its first reading; no source found records what became of it.

verdicts.claim: Amendments to motions had to be submitted in writing rather than raised orally, under Bill 86-2-S, introduced 28 January 1986.
verdicts.note: The bill and the date are right. TopSCHOLAR sga/Legislation/Bills/45 is "Bill 86-2-S - Amendments to Written Motions", dated 28-1-1986, described as a bill regarding amending written motions in lieu of oral amendments. The over-claim is "had to be": the source is a bill, that is a proposal, and nothing on the record shows it passed. The page carries a second date of 4 February 1986, a week later, but I will not guess what that field means.
verdicts.fixed: Bill 86-2-S, introduced 28 January 1986, would have required amendments to motions to be submitted in writing rather than raised orally. Whether it passed is not recorded in any source found.

verdicts.claim: Bill 86-1-F, introduced 9 September 1986, proposed major and minor representatives, carrying forward the college representative seats the outgoing congress had created in March 1986.
verdicts.note: The first half is exactly right: sga/Legislation/Bills/64 is "Bill 86-1-F - College Representative Elections", dated 9-9-1986, described as a bill proposing major/minor representatives. The trailing clause is unsourced. The cited page says nothing about March 1986 or about carrying anything forward. The Bills listing does show spring 1986 measures in the area (Bill 86-19-S on voting of representatives for colleges, Bill 86-32-S on fall election of graduate college representatives) but neither is dated to March and neither is cited here.
verdicts.fixed: Bill 86-1-F, introduced 9 September 1986, proposed major and minor representatives.

verdicts.claim: Bill #89-01-F, introduced 5 September 1989, amended the by-laws concerning the President's Board and dealt with committee assignments.
verdicts.note: Title, date and subject all confirmed at sga/Legislation/Bills/123: "Bill #89-01-F - Bylaw Amendment Concerning President's Board", dated 5-9-1989, described as a bill regarding committee assignments. The single over-claim is the verb: the source records a bill proposing a by-law amendment, not an amendment that took effect. Nothing found shows it passed.
verdicts.fixed: Bill #89-01-F, introduced 5 September 1989, proposed a by-law amendment concerning the President's Board and dealt with committee assignments.

verdicts.claim: Bill #90-1-F amended the by-laws on the sponsorship of bills and resolutions.
verdicts.note: sga/Legislation/Bills/128 is "Bill #90-1-F - Bylaw Amendment Concerning Sponsorship of Bills / Resolutions", described as a bill regarding sponsorship of bills and resolutions. The page carries only the year 1990, no month or day, which is why the fact wisely gives no date. Same verb problem as the entry above: a bill proposing an amendment is not an amendment made.
verdicts.fixed: Bill #90-1-F, in autumn 1990, proposed a by-law amendment on the sponsorship of bills and resolutions.

verdicts.claim: The president held a veto and Congress could override it. Bill #91-6-S changed the by-law governing the override, and the procedure was used on 14 March 1991 when a resolution on emergency kits survived a veto.
verdicts.note: Two separate strands, one stronger than the fact makes it and one weaker. The bill is confirmed beyond the cited source: sga/Legislation/Bills/135 is "Bill #91-6-S - By-Laws" and TopSCHOLAR describes it as a bill regarding overriding vetoes, so the fact should cite that page rather than a Herald headline. The event strand over-reaches. The headline at Herald 66:49, 14 Mar 1991 (dlsc_ua_records/7758) reads "Emergency Kit Resolution Survives Veto - Associated Student Government" and nothing more; the article was not read. 14 March 1991 is the publication date, so the vote preceded it, and the headline does not say an override procedure was used or that Congress voted. The resolution is identifiable as Resolution 91-2-S, Emergency Equipment (Resolutions/182), described as placing emergency road kits in university vehicles.
verdicts.fixed: The president held a veto. Bill #91-6-S, in spring 1991, was a by-law bill on overriding vetoes. The Herald of 14 March 1991 reported that a resolution on emergency road kits had survived a veto; the article was not read, so the date and manner of that vote are not established.

verdicts.claim: Congress had 32 positions in spring 1988, of which 2 were contested at the filing deadline.
verdicts.note: The headline at Herald 63:47, 22 Mar 1988 (dlsc_ua_records/7490) reads "2 of 32 Associated Student Government Positions Contested", confirmed on the landing page. Two changes of meaning. The source counts Associated Student Government positions, which is wider than Congress and on the evidence of the same issue includes the executive - it also indexes a presidential candidate item. And "at the filing deadline" is nowhere in the source; the fact supplies a moment the Herald does not.
verdicts.fixed: The Herald of 22 March 1988 reported that 2 of 32 Associated Student Government positions were contested.

verdicts.claim: Congress seats were filled by three routes: election alongside the executive each April, fall elections held in October including a separate freshman election, and filing followed by a vote of Congress at a meeting to fill seats left empty.
verdicts.note: The three routes are all real for this period, but the single cited source carries only the third. Herald 63:37, 4 Feb 1988 (7471) is "4 Student Government Association Congress Positions Filled at Meeting" and says nothing about April or October. The April route and the fall route are evidenced elsewhere in this archive but are not cited here, and the fall evidence is thin: Herald 67:13, 10 Oct 1991 is "Associated Student Government Elections Tuesday", an advance notice rather than a report, and the 27 September 1990 issue indexes a freshman candidates item. The fact also asserts "filing" as part of the third route; the headline does not mention filing.
verdicts.fixed: Seats could be filled by a vote of Congress at a meeting: the Herald of 4 February 1988 reported four congress positions filled that way. Members were also elected with the executive each April, and further seats, including freshman seats, were filled in fall elections.

verdicts.claim: A member could lose his seat for absenteeism. Nick Hicks lost his seat in October 1987, and the body moved to get tough on absenteeism the following week.
verdicts.note: Both events are real but the fact welds them into a causal chain the sources do not support. Herald 63:17, 22 Oct 1987 (dlsc_ua_records/6878) carries exactly "Associated Student Government Member Loses Seat - Nick Hicks" and gives no reason at all. The absenteeism item is a different issue and a different uncited source: Herald 63:18, 27 Oct 1987 (6877), "Associated Student Government to Get Tough on Absenteeism". That is the next issue, five days later, not quite "the following week". Both dates are publication dates. This archive's own 1987-88 record shows a second seat lost that October, Bill Schilling's, and attributes it to a hall association refusing him leave, which is a further reason not to assume absenteeism was the general mechanism.
verdicts.fixed: The Herald of 22 October 1987 reported that a member, Nick Hicks, had lost his seat; the report gives no reason. The next issue, 27 October, reported that the body would get tough on absenteeism.

verdicts.claim: The only surviving consolidated text of the founding framework is "Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments," dated 4 August 1986, the single document in which twenty years of amendments to the 1966 constitution were gathered.
verdicts.note: The document and its date are confirmed: sga/Constitution/Constitution/2 is "Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments", dated 4-8-1986. Everything else is unsupported. "The only surviving" and "the single document" are superlatives with no source, and the same series holds sga/Constitution/Constitution/1, "Constitution of WKU Associated Students", so a second Associated Students constitutional text does survive. "Twenty years of amendments to the 1966 constitution were gathered" is read off the words "with Amendments" in the title; the researcher states in his own notes that the PDF would not open, so no one has seen what is in it.
verdicts.fixed: A consolidated text, "Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments," is dated 4 August 1986 and sits in the SGA records alongside an earlier unamended Associated Students constitution. Its contents were not read.

verdicts.claim: A Judicial Council existed alongside Congress in this period; its membership roster for 1986-87 survives in the SGA records, dated August 1986.
verdicts.note: Confirmed at sga/Documents/Reports/9: "Judicial Council Roster, 1986-87", described as the membership of the Judicial Council for the 1986-1987 school year, with a start date of August 1986 and an end date of May 1987. The claim is carefully limited to the roster's existence and date and does not over-read it, which is the right call given that the roster itself was not opened.

verdicts.claim: Holding a paid university staff post made an officer ineligible under the ASG constitution: Amos Gott resigned as Judicial Council chairman in January 1991 after taking a part-time university job.
verdicts.note: This is the weakest fact in the block. The cited headline, confirmed on the landing page for Herald 66:33, 17 Jan 1991 (dlsc_ua_records/7730), reads "Two Associated Student Government Officers Step Down - Amos Gott, Van Hodge". That is all of it. It supports two officers stepping down and it names Gott. It does not support the office he held, the part-time job, or a constitutional ineligibility rule - three claims built out of a headline whose article was never read. The Judicial Council chairmanship in particular is the archive's warned-against move of treating a council or committee chair as an officer in order to hang a rule on him. Gott is recorded in data/years.json as ASG president for 1989-90, so by January 1991 he was a past president, which makes his office that January a question rather than an assumption.
verdicts.fixed: The Herald of 17 January 1991 reported that two Associated Student Government officers, Amos Gott and Van Hodge, had stepped down. The headline gives neither their offices nor their reasons, and the article was not read.

verdicts.claim: Constitutional amendments were put to the student body for ratification. On 12 November 1987, 81 students voted to approve a set of amendments.
verdicts.note: The headline is exact - Herald 63:23, 12 Nov 1987 (dlsc_ua_records/7317), "81 Students Vote to Approve Student Government Association Amendments" - and the count of 81 is genuinely in the source. The date is wrong in kind: 12 November 1987 is the publication date, so the vote had already happened when the paper appeared. The block's own notes flag that the archive's "Student Government Association" label in these years is the indexer's later usage, since the body was still the Associated Students until fall 1992, so the fact should not carry that name forward either.
verdicts.fixed: Constitutional amendments were put to the student body. The Herald of 12 November 1987 reported that 81 students had voted to approve a set of amendments.

verdicts.claim: Amendments also required a threshold of members present inside Congress: an amendment was defeated on 9 April 1987 because too few members turned up to vote on it.
verdicts.note: The headline is confirmed on the landing page for Herald 62:52, 9 Apr 1987 (dlsc_ua_records/5913): "Amendment is Defeated by Low Member Turnout - Associated Student Government". Two over-claims. The date is the issue date, not the day of the vote. And "required a threshold of members present" states a constitutional rule that the headline does not contain and that the researcher himself lists under "not established", noting no source gives the quorum figure. A defeat by low turnout is evidence that turnout mattered, not evidence of a stated threshold.
verdicts.fixed: The Herald of 9 April 1987 reported an amendment defeated by low member turnout. No source found states what threshold applied.

verdicts.claim: Congress voted to expand itself on 29 March 1990, a week after reporting it might add representatives, so that classes and student groups would have more voice.
verdicts.note: Well sourced in its spine and loose at both ends. The headline at Herald 65:49, 29 Mar 1990 (dlsc_ua_records/7629) is "Associated Student Government Votes to Expand Congress", confirmed, and the trailing week is real: Herald 65:47, 22 Mar 1990 (7628) carries "Associated Student Government May Add Representatives", though the fact does not cite it. Two faults. 29 March 1990 is the publication date, so the vote preceded it. And "so that classes and student groups would have more voice" is a motive that appears in neither headline; the archive's rule is not to guess at motive. The resulting seat count is nowhere recorded, as the researcher notes.
verdicts.fixed: The Herald of 29 March 1990 reported that Congress had voted to expand itself, a week after the issue of 22 March reported that it might add representatives. No source found records the resulting seat count or whether the expansion took effect.

verdicts.claim: The renaming was carried out as a constitutional amendment: Bill #92-10-S, introduced 1 April 1992, was a bill to change Associated Student Government to Student Government Association.
verdicts.note: Confirmed exactly at sga/Legislation/Bills/149: "Bill #92-10-S - Constitutional Amendment to Rename ASG to SGA", dated 1-4-1992, described as a bill to change Associated Student Government to Student Government Association. Title, date and characterisation as a constitutional amendment all come straight off the record. Worth an editor's note that the Bills listing also holds Bill #92-14-S, "Constitutional Amendments", in the same term, so the rename was not the only constitutional business that spring.

verdicts.claim: The Associated Students voted to rename itself on 7 April 1992; students approved the change in a referendum on 14 April 1992; it became effective in fall 1992.
verdicts.note: The WKU SGA history page states it in those terms: the Associated Students voted on 7 April 1992 to change its name to the Student Government Association, the change was approved in an April 14 student referendum, and it became effective in fall 1992. The fact does not over-read it. One caution for the editor rather than a fault in the fact: this is a later compiled page, which this archive ranks below a contemporaneous source, and it gives no turnout figure - which is where the summary's invented "about 1,200" comes from.

verdicts.claim: A four-college representative structure with required alternates was in place by November 1992: Bill #92-13-F, introduced 17 November 1992, appointed the required alternate representatives for the four college representatives.
verdicts.note: The bill is exactly as cited: sga/Legislation/Bills/147 is "Bill #92-13-F - Appointment of Alternate for the Four College Representatives", dated 17-11-1992, described as a bill to appoint the required alternate representatives. The title does carry the four-college structure and the word required. The over-claim is the verb again: a bill proposing appointments is not appointments made, and nothing found shows it passed. This fact also sits outside the block's stated range of 1986-87 to 1991-92 and is labelled 1992-93, so it belongs in the block only as forward context.
verdicts.fixed: Bill #92-13-F, introduced 17 November 1992, proposed the appointment of the required alternates for the four college representatives, so a four-college representative structure was in place by that date.

verdicts.claim: Congress gave awards to its own members at a yearly banquet. The minutes of 15 March 1988 carry a description of awards listing the Dero Downing Award, Outstanding Congress Member, Outstanding Committee Member, the Dean Charles A. Keown Award, the Kerrie Faye Stewart Memorial Award and the Mary Angela Norcia Award.
verdicts.note: The list is verbatim correct. The TopSCHOLAR description for sga/Meetings/Minutes/60, dated 15-3-1988, names all six in that order. The framing sentence goes past it. The source is a description of awards attached to a set of minutes; it says nothing about a banquet, nothing about it being yearly, and nothing about who the recipients were - two of the six are named for a university president and a dean, so "to its own members" is not safe for the whole list. The banquet is corroborated elsewhere in this archive, at Herald 63:39, 11 Feb 1988, but that source is not cited here.
verdicts.fixed: The minutes of 15 March 1988 carry a description of awards listing the Dero Downing Award, Outstanding Congress Member, Outstanding Committee Member, the Dean Charles A. Keown Award, the Kerrie Faye Stewart Memorial Award and the Mary Angela Norcia Award.

rewritten:
The third branch of the Associated Student Government in these years was the Judicial Council. The fullest account of it the archive holds is a typescript constitution TopSCHOLAR dates to 1986, "Constitution of WKU Associated Students with Amendments", bound with an undated sheet of amendments. What follows describes that document. How far its terms reach across this period is not established here: Paul J. Deom's letter of February 1982 cites the judicial provisions as article IX, so a differently numbered text governed in 1980-82, and twenty-one amendments students approved on 11 November 1987 took effect only after the spring 1988 elections.

In that text, Article I, Section 2 divided ASG into an executive branch, a legislative branch, a judicial branch and committees established by the president and by Congress, and Article IV, Section 1 vested the judicial authority in the Judicial Council. The council had seven regular members and three alternates, appointed by the ASG president with the approval of a two-thirds vote of the full membership of Congress and taking office no later than two weeks after the fall term began, though Article II, Section 3 of the same document says judicial appointments needed only a simple majority. The president named the chairman from among the seven; the chairman presided, set the time and place of meetings, and administered the oath of office to ASG's officers and to Congress. The council elected one alternate as clerk, its records were kept in the ASG office, and alternates were designated first, second and third and filled vacancies in that order. A member had to have attended Western the semester immediately preceding, remain a student and not a faculty or staff member for the whole term, stay off disciplinary probation, hold an academic standing of 2.25 or higher, sit outside Congress, and not have been a candidate for an ASG executive office in the year of appointment. The base text appointed three persons each academic year to a one-year term; the amendment sheet raised that to seven, and rewrote two of the qualifications.

Five duties were listed: to interpret and clarify the constitution and by-laws at the request of the Executive Council, the president or Congress; to hear appeals from inferior courts; to exercise judicial review over acts of Congress at the request of a Congress member, the president, the Executive Council or any registered student; to hear all appeals from the Rules and Elections Committee over election disputes, including qualifications for candidacy; and to set its own procedural rules and ethical considerations. A council member or alternate could be removed for just cause by a three-quarters vote of the full membership of Congress acting as a judicial body, on the written endorsement of five members of Congress or five of the council, with no final vote until fourteen days had passed; the amendment sheet lowered that to two-thirds. Impeachment of executive officers and of Congress members was Congress's own work, by a two-thirds vote of its full membership on the written endorsement of five congressional members, again after fourteen days. The Rules and Elections Committee decided election disputes subject only to appeal to the council.

What the archive records of the council at work is intermittent. Deom wrote in February 1982 that Steve Fuller had appointed him in autumn 1980 on the understanding of a two-year term, that the executive council and the president had decided to replace him, and that the report of a new council being named each January was wrong. Marcel Bush called the council "virtually non-functioning", said it had met once to her knowledge in her three years in ASG, said two of the seven seats were active when she became president, and said she told David Payne after her resignation to appoint a new council as soon as possible. Six of the seven appointees were sworn in at the ASG meeting of Tuesday 26 January 1982 - chairman Gale Williams, Bob Dillard, Regenia Giles, Rick Murphy, Dave Hoffmann and Jill Capps - with Archie Beck absent and to be sworn in later; three alternates were also appointed. Margaret Ragan, administrative vice president, said the council was made up of students who had never served on ASG or run for an executive office, and the report added that members served one year and that the council would hold one scheduled meeting a year but could meet whenever a controversy arose.

In March 1987 Greg Robertson, vice chairman of the Rules and Elections Committee, described the council as ASG's judicial authority and as the body a disqualified candidate was appealing to; in that election 38 candidates filed for 41 seats and 25 were unopposed, against 20 of 44 unopposed the year before. A roster survives for 1986-87: seven regular members, Kent Groemling, Bill Schilling, Naheed Shafi, Jerry Castleberry, Dwight Austion, Jennifer Borsch and Dan Wooten as chair, and three alternates, Stacey Crain, Keith Wallace and Mary Kate Erwin. Amos Gott, ASG president in 1989-90, chaired the council in 1990-91 and resigned in January 1991 after a new part-time job as adviser for fraternity affairs made him ineligible; the Herald reported that the ASG constitution bars faculty and staff members from serving.
problems:
The summary cannot go out as written. Seven problems, in order of seriousness.

1. It reads a headline against the story beneath it. "David Payne appointed a full council in January 1982 ... and had seven members sworn in on 26 January" comes from the lede of the 28 January 1982 report. The body of that same story names six taking the oath and says Archie Beck was absent and would be sworn in later. Six, not seven.

2. A name is wrong. "chaired by Dan Woolen" should be Dan Wooten. The 1986-87 roster is clean typewriting and reads "Dan Wooten-Chair". The same document reads "Dwight Austion", not Auslion.

3. It states numbers no fact in the structure carries. The whole April 1982 sentence, "989 votes were recorded against 937 signatures" and the rejected bid to disqualify Ragan over late spending forms, rests on Herald 57:55, 15 April 1982, which appears nowhere in the structure array and has no URL anywhere in the block. I read that issue and the figures are right (dlsc_ua_records/2464), but the archive cannot publish them off an uncited source. Either add a structure entry with that URL or cut the sentence. The same sentence also over-attributes: the report says the elections "were not certified", it does not say the Rules and Elections Committee refused to certify them.

4. Two further summary claims outrun their structure entries even though the underlying URL is in the block. "Ed Kenney appealed his 1987 disqualification" is true and is at fact 18's URL, but fact 18 never names him. "Bruce Cambron appealed to it in April 1988 after 380 write-in ballots were ruled invalid" is true and is on the same page as fact 22's source, but no structure fact carries the 380 figure or the appeal. Both need their own entries before the summary can lean on them.

5. It implies a settled arrangement running the whole twelve years where the archive shows the opposite. Paragraphs two and three describe "the constitution" flatly for 1980-81 through 1991-92, but the only constitutional text read is a typescript TopSCHOLAR dates to 1986, bound with an undated amendment sheet. Deom's February 1982 letter cites the judicial provisions as article IX, section 2, subsection B, paragraph 5, so a differently numbered text governed in 1980-82; and the block's own fact 20 records twenty-one amendments taking effect after the spring 1988 elections. The summary must say which document it is describing and stop short of the years it cannot cover.

6. It characterises the body. "The council worked in bursts" is a judgement about the organisation rather than a record of what it did, and "Marcel Bush made no appointments in autumn 1981" states as settled fact something that was contested in the paper: it is David Payne's assertion, while Bush said two of the seven seats were active and that nobody had worried about reappointing members who had dropped out or graduated.

7. Smaller point, but it should be fixed at the same time. The summary presents the appointment rule as a two-thirds vote of Congress without noting that Article II, Section 3 A.9 of the same document says judicial appointments need only a simple majority; and it gives the qualifications and the seven-member composition without noting the amendment sheet alters two of the qualifications and the base text appointed three members a year, not seven.

Two structure entries do not appear in the summary at all and probably do not belong in a judicial-branch block: fact 21 (nine open Congress seats, December 1987) has no judicial content, and fact 22 stands as background to the Cambron appeal the summary asserts but the structure does not support.

Also correct the unanswered section: item 1 says the 1982 member's surname is illegible. It is not. The page image reads "Jill Capps, a Bowling Green sophomore." Item 2's caution about no surviving rulings still stands; I found none either.

claims_rejected.claim: Paul J. Deom wrote that he had been appointed to the Judicial Council in autumn 1980 by then-president Steve Fuller on the understanding that he would serve a three-year term under article IX, section 1, subsection B, paragraph 1 of the constitution then in force, and that the executive council and president had decided to replace him. He also disputed the report that a new council was appointed each January, citing the constitution's requirement that members take office no later than two weeks after the fall term.
claims_rejected.note: Two errors, both readable in the page image at 6x. The letter says 'a two-year term', not three, and cites 'article IX, section 2, subsection B, paragraph 5', not section 1 subsection B paragraph 1. The rest is right: appointed in fall 1980 by then-president Steve Fuller; 'Since the executive council and the president have decided to replace me'; and he names Margaret Ragan as the source of the every-January claim he is disputing. rewritten:
SGA's judicial branch in these years was the Judicial Council. The constitution vested the association's judicial authority in it, and the council had five justices throughout the period. The president appointed them and the legislative body confirmed each by a two-thirds vote; the president also named the chief justice from among the five, subject to a majority vote. Justices took office no later than two weeks after the fall term began and served one academic year, and vacancies were to be filled within two weeks of a resignation. A justice needed a 2.5 cumulative grade point average. The council picked one justice as clerk at its first meeting.

The rulebook did not stay still. Under the constitution as amended spring 2001, still posted on SGA's site in November 2004, judicial review ran over the acts of Congress, a justice reported to Congress once a month, and a justice was barred from sitting in Congress. The text proposed in spring 2005 extended judicial review to the Executive Cabinet and the Senate at the request of any registered student not on the council, broadened the bar to any other branch of SGA, set the council to meet no less than twice a month, and added a requirement that a justice have completed a year as an elected or appointed SGA officer unless the Senate granted an exemption. By the version posted in October 2012 that qualification had gone, the chief justice had instead to have served a year as an associate justice, and the reporting duty had become twice a month. No source found here dates those changes.

The council's other written powers were steady. It interpreted the constitution and bylaws on request, heard election appeals and questions of candidacy, enacted and reviewed the election codes subject to a majority vote of the legislative body, and reviewed every constitutional amendment before that body voted on it. It acted under the attendance policy: senators were allowed no more than three absences a semester unless the council excused them, and the Speaker referred a senator with excessive absences, or one already censured, to the council, which had to meet and decide within seven days. A request signed by no fewer than ten students obliged the council to investigate an executive or legislative officer for censure, censure being defined in the bylaws as an act of the council expressing disapproval of an officer's action; a request against a justice went to the other four, with the president presiding and breaking ties. The chief justice presided over impeachments of executive and legislative officers and administered the oath of office. A justice could be removed only by the Senate, on the written endorsement of a fifth of its membership and a two-thirds vote of its full membership, with the Speaker in the chair.

The election codes adopted on 22 January 2004 made the council the supervisor of all SGA elections. They required a candidate orientation meeting, with disqualification for a candidate who failed to attend unless the council granted an exemption; set spending limits from $450 for president down to $50 for legislative candidates; required itemised expenditure reports filed with the council; gave three business days after the results for appeals, protests and disqualifications; and required a new election if a majority of the council found an impropriety. The council met once a week during a campaign and reported its rulings to the legislature.

No Judicial Council minutes survive for this decade, and what is known of the council's work comes from SGA's senate minutes, its own posted opinions and the Herald. In February 2009, after a resignation left the student regent seat empty, the council applied the clause that gave the executive vice president the presidency but not the Board of Regents seat and required a special election for the seat under KRS 164.321, with the council holding discretion over the timeline, applications and campaigning. The Herald of 12 February 2009 reported that the council voted 2-1 on 10 February to hold that election, that Chief Justice Lisa Kappler cast the dissent, and that she resigned two days later in a letter saying she wanted to spend more time on school and family. The Herald of 10 November 2009 reported the council removing one senator for unexcused absences and reviewing a second who was allowed to remain. The Herald of 15 November 2011 reported that ten of the senate's 36 members had been called before the council over the fall semester and that two were dismissed after failing to attend their hearings. In April 2013 the council disqualified the president-elect 3-2 over an election-code violation, then met again and decided unanimously not to contest the administrator's memorandum reinstating her, saying it did not believe it had the power to do so while recording its disapproval.

Two further rulings fell in 2013. On 29 August the council ruled unconstitutional a proposed amendment adding an international student senate seat, before the Senate voted on it; its authors, the president and the executive vice president, reworded it and the Senate passed the revision the following month. On 21 November the council ruled unconstitutional a senator's motion reversing SGA's support for a Talisman student fee, and ruled the 2005 policy behind that support unconstitutional as well.

The written office changed at the end of the period. Amendments the Senate adopted on 26 February 2013 and referred to the spring 2013 ballot made a justice's term the length of the justice's academic career, gave the council review over the enactments and impeachment proceedings of regional affiliates, and let it open a censure investigation on a majority of its own members rather than only on a ten-student request. A draft the council posted in 2014 would have raised it to seven justices, moved the choice of chief justice from the president to a majority of the justices serving in the spring, and created an associate chief justice. An amendment on those lines passed the Senate in February 2014 but was declared unconstitutional afterwards by the Executive Council, which found too few senators had been present for the vote to count, and the SGA website still described a five-justice council when the judicial page was last modified on 5 March 2014. All three changes appear in the constitution as amended spring 2017. Nothing found here shows when between 2014 and 2017 they took effect.
problems:
The structure is in unusually good shape: 24 of 27 facts are exactly supported, and the three I marked "trim" are true but under-cited or mis-linked rather than wrong. Nothing was unreachable. The summary is the problem, and it fails on five of the six listed tests.

1. Dates, numbers and counts the facts do not carry. The whole third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph rest on events that appear nowhere in "structure": the November 2009 removal, the November 2011 review of ten of 36 senators, the April 2013 3-2 disqualification, the September and December 2013 rulings, the February 2009 2-1 vote and the chief justice's resignation, and the February 2014 voiding. I found all of them in data/years.json with Herald citations, so they are not invented, but as the block stands the summary asserts a dozen figures and dates that its own evidence array cannot back. Either facts get added to "structure" or those sentences come out.

2. Two of those dates are wrong, and wrong in the same way: the Herald's publication date has been read as the date of the event. "It struck down a senate amendment in September 2013" - the council's ruling was 29 August 2013 (the Herald of 6 Sep 2013 says the council rejected it "on Aug. 29"); the Herald simply reported it on 3 September. "Voided a senate motion on Talisman funding in December 2013" - the ruling was 21 November 2013; the Herald reported it on 3 December.

3. It reads a headline as though it were the article beneath it, and gets the actors wrong. The September 2013 item was not "a senate amendment" the council struck down: it was a proposed amendment authored by the president and the executive vice president, which the council reviewed before the senate voted, under the very clause the summary itself cites (4.5.9). The senate then passed the reworded version. The summary reverses the sequence and attributes the amendment to the body that had not yet voted on it. Separately, "An amendment to raise the council to seven justices was voided in February 2014" leaves the agent out of a sentence in a Judicial Council block, so it reads as the council's own act; the archive says the Executive Council declared it unconstitutional after the meeting, on a quorum ground.

4. Superlative and characterisation without a source. "Its largest single act was in February 2009" is an unsourced superlative and a judgement about importance. "Most of its recorded work was elections and attendance" is a claim about the shape of a record that, by the block's own unanswered note, is missing entirely: no Judicial Council minutes survive for this decade.

5. It implies continuity the sources contradict. Paragraphs one and two present a single fixed rulebook for 2004-05 through 2013-14, but the rules changed inside the block and the block's own sources show it. In the 2001 constitution, still posted in November 2004 and cited as the block's first fact, judicial review ran over the acts of Congress only, a justice reported once a month, there was no "not in the Judicial Council" limitation, and a justice was barred only from Congress rather than from any other branch. The spring 2005 text still says once a month. Only the October 2012 text says twice a month. So "designated a justice to report to the senate twice a month" and "judicial review over acts of the Executive Cabinet and the Senate" are not true of the years the block opens with. The summary also says "the senate confirmed each by a two-thirds vote" for a period that opens with a body the constitution called Congress.

6. Smaller things: "a dean's memorandum" gives Howard Bailey a title the 2013 source does not; the archive calls him dean of Student Life in 2004, nine years earlier. And the April 2013 sentence drops the two facts that make the episode legible - the council's decision not to contest was unanimous, and its stated ground was that it did not believe it had the power.

I have written a corrected summary. It keeps the narrative but pins every date to the ruling rather than the report, names the acting body in each case, drops the superlative and the characterisations, and separates what was constant across the decade from what changed. If the editors want the summary to rest only on "structure", the fifth and sixth paragraphs of the rewrite must be cut and matching facts added to the array first.
