rewritten:
The judicial branch of the Student Government Association was the Judicial Council. The constitution vested SGA's judicial authority in it, set it at seven justices, and made them presidential appointees confirmed by a two-thirds vote of the Senate. A justice had to be in good standing with the university, be a student for the whole term of office, and not belong to another branch, and held the seat for the duration of an academic career while meeting the requirements of the office. The council appointed its own chief justice by majority vote, subject to a majority of the Senate, and the chief justice appointed an associate chief justice, also approved by the Senate. A chief justice had to have completed a year as an associate justice, or be granted an exemption by the Senate. That wording stood in the 2017, 2023-24 and 2024-25 texts, and the council page published in 2026 described the branch the same way.

The council's duties were to interpret the constitution and bylaws on request, to exercise judicial review of Executive Cabinet and Senate actions at the request of any registered student not on the council, to rule on the absences and office hours of senators and officers, to enact and review election codes subject to a Senate vote, to run the code meetings candidates had to attend, to hear election complaints, and to hold censure hearings. Under the General Procedural Rules the Senate adopted in spring 2022, quorum was five members minus the number of vacancies. The bill supporting their adoption recorded that the council had previously had no formal written guidelines or procedures for its functions and duties.

The branch's own record is unevenly published, and this account does not cover the whole period. No minutes, opinions or roster survive for 2014-15 or 2016-17, and the roster posted for 2015-16 carries no date. Written opinions were posted only for Fall 2012 to April 2014. Minutes are posted for 2017-18, 2019-20 and 2021-22 through 2025-26, with a single file for 2020-21 and two opinions for 2018-19.

Where the record survives, the council ruled against other parts of SGA. On 21 November 2013, in Opinion 2013FA-006, it held that Bill 08-05-S of 2005, the Talisman student referendum, had never been passed by a route the bylaws authorised, was unconstitutional when passed and had never represented SGA's position, which also made the Senate's vote the same day to rescind it null. On 3 December 2015 it voided Bills 8-15-F and 9-15-F under Bylaw 6.1, because SGA could allocate money only to students, cancelling $1,500 for the physics department and up to $759 for art. On 3 December 2021 it held that where the constitution and the bylaws conflicted over the executive veto the constitution governed, and that the bylaws had to be amended to match. On 12 November 2025, in a hearing recorded as The Executive Cabinet v. Ismail, it declined by 7-0 to censure Senator Jade Ismail.

Several chief justices left office mid-year. Kelsey Luttrell announced in December 2015 that she would step down at the end of the semester, saying the council had been publicly ridiculed and lacked support. Jacob McAndrews announced in March 2019 that he would resign to run for elected office. Erika Puhakka stepped down in March 2021, and President Garrett Edmonds left the seat for his successor. Ellen Henderson swore in Associate Chief Justice Morgan Gammons as chief justice in November 2024 before graduating, and Blake Graham stepped down in November 2025 after Sophie Stirling was elected to succeed him.

The council's duties grew by amendment, mostly on legislation written outside it. Bills 1-17-F and 2-17-F, both authored by Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell and given first reading on 28 August 2017, added a temporary committee of the three branches for formulating constitutional amendments and the updating of the constitution after student body referendums, and made the chief justice interim speaker of the Senate when the speaker was absent or removed. Bills 12-23-F and 15-23-F, authored by Chief Justice Isaac King and given first reading on 14 November 2023, raised the chief justice's office hours from one to five a week and required every member of the council to keep two office hours a month. Four further bills given first reading on 12 March 2024, written by four senators with King, Associate Chief Justice Ellen Henderson and Associate Justice Garrison Reed, made the chief justice report to the Senate weekly, required a chief justice to be eligible to serve a full academic year or resign at the end of their last full one, raised the judicial grade point floor from 2.0 to 2.5, and required removal of any member censured twice in the same academic year. The council applied that last rule on 6 November 2024, censuring Malick Ibrahim, Myricle Gholston and Karisha Petty a second time each for unexcused absences and removing all three by 7-0 votes.

By 2026 the election role was set out in detail. The spring 2026 election codes required the council to meet once a week during the election season, barred a justice from advocating for or against a candidate or giving a candidate an official interpretation of SGA policy without a council ruling, including by liking, sharing or commenting on campaign posts, and required every candidate to attend one of two code meetings on pain of disqualification unless the council granted an exemption. The bylaws codified on 24 February 2026 sent any senator with two unexcused absences in a semester to the council for an attendance hearing, and made the chief justice the presiding officer at Senate trials for committee chair removals, expulsions from the Senate, and executive or judicial impeachments.
problems:
Four separate problems, and the first is structural rather than cosmetic.

1. More than half the summary rests on nothing in the structure array. The whole of paragraph three and the whole of paragraph four, plus the closing clause about three senators, cite no fact in the block. Not one of these names, dates or figures appears anywhere in the thirty facts: the 3 December 2015 voiding of Bills 8-15-F and 9-15-F with $1,500 for physics and up to $759 for art; the 3 December 2021 ruling on the executive veto; the 12 November 2025 Ismail hearing and its 7-0 outcome; Kelsey Luttrell, Jacob McAndrews, Erika Puhakka, Garrett Edmonds, Ellen Henderson and Blake Graham leaving office; and the removal of three senators on 6 November 2024. The 21 November 2013 Talisman holding is carried only by a source label, never by a fact. I chased every one of them down and they are all true, which is the good news: the 2015 rulings and Luttrell's resignation are in data/years.json from two Herald reports of 3 December 2015; the veto ruling is in the Judicial Council minutes of 3 December 2021 at /sga/2018-2019-judicial/21-22-judicial-minutes/jc_min_12_3_21.docx and reads almost exactly as the summary has it; the Ismail hearing is at /sga/2025_2026_judicial/jc_minutes/hearing_11_12.docx, captioned The Executive Cabinet v. Ismail with six executive plaintiffs and a unanimous 7-0 refusal to censure; the three removals are in the minutes of 6 November 2024, each senator censured twice and terminated under section 4.6.12. But a block cannot be published on facts its checker had to go and find. Every one of those sources needs adding to the structure array before this goes out.

2. Characterisation instead of description, in three places. 'It ruled against SGA itself throughout' is a verdict on the body, and 'throughout' asserts a pattern from four scattered rulings in a record that is completely silent for 2014-15 and 2016-17 and undated for 2015-16. 'Chief justices often did not finish a year' does the same with 'often'. 'The council also enlarged its own duties' is the third, and it is also wrong on the facts, which brings me to the next point.

3. It credits the council with bills other people wrote. Bills 1-17-F and 2-17-F, the two 2017 amendments the summary says the council used to enlarge its own duties, were both authored by Conner Hounshell, Chief of Staff, an executive officer, and sponsored by the Student Affairs committee. No justice authored either. The 2024 amendments are a milder version of the same error: the summary presents them as the council enlarging itself, when Bills 24, 25, 26 and 29-24-S were led by four senators, Meghan Pierce, Samantha Bodemann, Hannah Evans and Joel Hornback, with three justices co-authoring. Relatedly, 'the entire executive cabinet's censure request' overstates the caption: the six plaintiffs include Speaker of the Senate Hadley Whipple, who is a legislative officer, and nothing establishes that the six were the whole cabinet.

4. It reads as an unbroken account of a period where the archive has large holes. The block is titled 2014-15 through 2026-27, yet there is no judicial record at all for 2014-15 and 2016-17, the 2015-16 roster carries no date, opinions stop in April 2014, and 2020-21 survives as one file. The researcher knows all this and says so honestly in the unanswered section, but the summary itself never tells the reader, so it implies continuity the sources do not carry. The sentence 'That was still the method in 2026' is the one continuity claim that does hold up, on the 2026 council page.

Two smaller matters carried up from the fact checks. The summary's line that quorum was five minus vacancies is right, but the neighbouring facts misstate the absence-excuse deadline and describe the procedural rules as granting the council a veto over the Senate, which they do not. And two facts are simply wrong and would have gone out uncorrected: the opinions page lists nineteen opinions, not eighteen, and the 2013-14 opinions do not show a settled council of five.

I have not touched data/years.json and have not run the build.

rewritten:
The Associated Students voted on 7 April 1992 to change its name to the Student Government Association. Students approved the change in a referendum on 14 April 1992 and it took effect in fall 1992. What the governing documents said between 1992 and 2000 is not established here; the archive records amendments on the ballot in 1993, 1996 and 1999 whose text has not survived.

The oldest governing document this pass could open is a constitution headed "As amended Spring 2001 Semester," posted on SGA's website and captured in November 2004, with six numbered amendments printed after its text. Its opening clause made every enrolled student a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections, a provision the archive elsewhere credits to the 2004 constitution but which the 2001 text already carried word for word. It set three branches: an executive branch of five officers, being the President, Executive Vice President and Vice Presidents of Finance, Public Relations and Administration; a legislative branch called Congress; and a five-member Judicial Council appointed by the president with the approval of two-thirds of Congress. The base text tied Congress seats to the four classes, to residence halls apportioned one to four by hall population, and to graduate, non-traditional and at-large members, with an Academic Council representative for each college, the Coordinator of Committees and every standing and ad hoc committee chair appointed by the president. Amendment 3 replaced that composition with a smaller one that dropped the non-traditional seats and added off-campus and academic-college representatives. Amendments needed two-thirds of the full Congress and a student referendum, and every constitutional change was subject to the university administration's approval. Amendment 6, a Supremacy Clause, is recorded on SGA's own results page as passed at the spring 2002 general election, with no vote total beside it. The bylaws posted alongside were headed "As Proposed Spring 2002 Semester"; no ratifying vote for them has been found.

Bill 03-5-S, "WWHR FM Student Referendum," is dated 25 February 2003 in SGA's legislation archive. The Herald reported that Congress voted only to put the question to students, not to impose a fee; that a yes vote would send a $3-a-semester fee for the campus radio station Revolution 91.7-WWHR to the Board of Regents for the final decision; and that executive vice president John Bradley expected the board to take it up at its 9 May 2003 quarterly meeting. Students approved the fee 1,066 to 765 in an election in which 2,014 voted, the result read out by chief justice Holly Skidmore shortly after 1 a.m. TopSCHOLAR's description of the 9 May 2003 quarterly minutes lists "library, facility improvement and radio station fees" among the agenda items, but the minutes themselves would not open, so what the board decided is not established here. A $9 Talisman yearbook fee put to students the same way in March 2005 passed 1,019 to 669, and its fate at the board is likewise unrecorded in this archive.

Bill 03-10-F, "New Constitution and Bylaws," is dated 10 November 2003 in the same archive. The constitution it carried is headed "As Proposed Fall 2003" and divides SGA into executive, legislative and judicial branches. The executive became a seven-member Executive Cabinet: President, Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President elected, and a Chief of Staff and Directors of Public Relations, Information Technology and Academic and Student Affairs appointed, all seven voting in cabinet. The Vice Presidencies of Finance and Public Relations disappeared. Congress became the Student Senate, fixed at thirty-five seats, four from each class, two graduate and seventeen at-large, with all but the four freshman and three at-large seats elected in the spring and any seat still vacant after the fall elections filled by presidential appointment with a majority of the Senate. A Speaker of the Senate, elected from the elected Senate by the previous semester's legislative branch, served as Coordinator of Committees, appointed the Secretary of the Senate and named the committee chairs subject to Senate approval. Five standing committees sat inside the legislative branch, and a new five-member Organizational-Aid Board dispensed aid to student organisations. The Executive Cabinet kept a veto over all Senate legislation, carried by a majority of the cabinet with written reasons to the sponsoring committee within forty-eight hours; the constitution set the override at three-fourths of the Senate while the bylaws set it at two-thirds of those present and voting, and the two documents were never reconciled. The bylaws fixed quorum at a simple majority, allowed a senator four absences a semester unless excused by the Judicial Council, and set meetings at 5 p.m. every Tuesday. On a presidential vacancy the Executive Vice President took the President's duties, but the student regent seat went to a special election of the student body under KRS 164.321, where the Spring 2001 constitution had filled the whole office that way. The amendment rule stayed at two-thirds of the Senate plus a referendum, but the clause subjecting constitutional change to the university administration's approval was dropped. Election Codes adopted on 22 January 2004 gave the Judicial Council charge of all elections, set filing between 1 February and 2 March, made a candidate orientation compulsory on pain of disqualification, and capped campaign spending from $450 for president down to $50 for legislative candidates, with no donor giving more than $100.

At the March 2005 general election students adopted a list of forty amendments compiled by the Legislative Research Committee, 1,193 to 262, and all twenty-five senate candidates on the ballot were elected to twenty-eight open seats. SGA afterwards posted a constitution headed "As Proposed Spring 2005"; no source found states that this document is the forty-amendment package. Against the 2004 text it raised the grade point average for a senate seat and for senate office from 2.0 to 2.5, lowered the veto override to two-thirds, moved the appointment of committee chairs from the Speaker to the President, raised the Speaker's minimum office hours from five to eight a week, seated the Speaker on the Executive Cabinet as an ex-officio non-voting member, required the Speaker to be at least a sophomore with a year's service as a senator, and added procedures for removing a committee head and for a vote of no confidence in the Speaker. The bylaws posted with it cut permitted absences from four a semester to three, raised the student University Senate representatives from three to five, required authors to defend their legislation before the Legislative Research Committee within two weeks, and corrected the fiscal record-keeping reference to Bill 02-07-F.

After that the governing record thins to nothing. SGA's senate minutes call the 2006-07 body "the fifth Student Government Association" without saying what the first was, and its rosters stayed under the constitutional thirty-five all year: eight of eighteen senators present on 5 September 2006, twenty-two of thirty-one on 28 November and sixteen of thirty-one on 5 December. No constitutional amendment, bylaw amendment or election-code revision between 2006 and 2010 turned up in this pass, which is an absence of evidence rather than evidence that nothing changed.
problems:
The structure is in good shape: 27 of 32 facts hold as written, and the five that need work need only trimming, not withdrawal. The summary is a different matter. It carries a large body of numbers, dates and names that no fact in the structure supports, and several of them are wrong.

Numbers and dates the facts do not carry. The whole fourth paragraph rests on one structure fact (Bill 03-10-F, dated 10 November 2003). Everything else in it is unsourced: that Robert Watkins wrote the documents, that he chaired the Legislative Research Committee, that he reviewed other universities' documents, "four attempts," "unanimously on 10 February 2004," "25 of 29 members there," "about 13 members struck from the roll," "9 March 2004," "132 students voted, 116 for and 16 against," "about 18,000," and "Executive officers were barred from proposing legislation." Two are checkable and fail: the archive's own record (data/years.json, 2004-03-16) reports 132 of about 18,000 voting but gives no 116-to-16 split anywhere, and the 116 figure that does exist in years.json belongs to a different year's amendment votes. "Fell from 75 seats to 35" is worse: no source gives Congress 75 seats, neither Spring 2001 composition sums to 75, and the archive's own December 2003 minutes entry puts Congress at 43 members. "Nine students stood for the 28 spring senate seats that month" appears to be the March 2005 figure (25 candidates, 28 open seats, structure fact 28) moved back a year and altered; nothing supports nine candidates in 2004.

Reading a headline as the article. The only Herald record of the February 2004 passage in data/herald-index-full.json is the index line "Student Government Association Approves New Constitution on Fifth Attempt" (12 February 2004), and for March the lines "Vote Set for Today" (9 March) and "Charter Passes" (11 March). The summary builds an attendance count, a roll purge, a vote split and a unanimity claim on top of headlines, which is precisely the failure CLAUDE.md warns about.

Continuity across years with no record. "The constitution SGA worked under for the rest of the decade was headed 'As amended Spring 2001 Semester'" places a 2001 document over the whole of the 1990s. It cannot have governed 1992 to 2000, and the block's own unanswered note 7 records amendments in 1993, 1996 and 1999 whose text is lost. "Nothing else in the governing documents changed with it," attached to the 1992 name change, is an unsourced negative that the same note contradicts.

A first-time claim without a source. "The Herald reported it as the first student referendum in SGA's history" has no structure fact behind it. The claim is real (data/years.json, 29 April 2003) but the block does not carry it, and a first-ever assertion published under the university's name needs its own citation.

Something asserted that the block itself says is unproven. "SGA published the resulting documents as its constitution and bylaws" states that the Spring 2005 documents are the 40-amendment package. Unanswered note 2 says in terms that no source establishes this. The summary cannot claim what the block's own caveats disclaim.

Two smaller errors of fact. "In February 2003 Congress passed Bill 03-5-S" reads the legislation index's date as a passage date; the Bill 02-07-F PDF proves that column is the drafting date (02-07-F is dated 11 October, first read 22 October, passed 3 December). And the October 2006 Division I-A football vote was a non-binding opinion poll run alongside the homecoming queen election, per data/years.json, not another instance of the fee-to-regents route the paragraph describes.

Finally, the block is scoped 1992 through 2010 but the summary stops in 2005 and drops the 2006-07 material entirely, including the senate numbering and the roster counts that the structure establishes.

verdicts.note: The heading is exact. But the heading says "As Proposed," and nothing found shows a ratifying vote, so "in force" is an inference the document does not carry. The block's own unanswered note 3 applies this same caution to the Spring 2005 bylaws; it should apply here too.

verdicts.claim: Bill 02-07-F, dated 11 October 2002 in SGA's own legislation archive, amended the bylaws of finance of the Student Government Association. The Spring 2005 bylaws cite it as the standard the chief financial officer must follow.
verdicts.note: The 2002 index reads "B 02-7-F: October 11, 2002: Amendment to the By-Laws of Finance." The bill PDF is still in Wayback and I opened it: bill date 11 October 2002, first reading 22 October, passed 3 December 2002, authors Nick Todd, Bob Bell, John Law. Spring 2005 bylaws, Article VII section 4, names Bill 02-07-F; the 2004 bylaws named 03-03-S. Both halves hold.

verdicts.claim: The fee referendum mechanism was created by Bill 03-5-S, "WWHR FM Student Referendum," dated 25 February 2003 in SGA's legislation archive. It placed a $3-per-semester fee question for campus radio station Revolution 91.7-WWHR on the 2-3 April 2003 general election ballot.
verdicts.fixed: Bill 03-5-S, "WWHR FM Student Referendum," is dated 25 February 2003 in SGA's legislation archive; the index carries only its number, date and title, and the bill's own PDF is not in the Wayback record. The Herald reported that the bill put a $3-per-semester fee question for campus radio station Revolution 91.7-WWHR on the 2-3 April 2003 general election ballot.
verdicts.note: The cited source is an index page: it gives number, date and title and nothing else. I tried the linked BIL03-05-S.pdf; the Wayback CDX record for that folder holds only index.html and R03-01-F.pdf, so the bill text is not retrievable. The $3, the station name and the 2-3 April ballot are real but come from the Herald of 4 March 2003, which I opened via Wayback. "The fee referendum mechanism was created by" is the researcher's framing; no source calls it a mechanism or says it created one. Also note that for Bill 02-07-F the index date proved to be the drafting date, not the passage date, so the 25 February date should not be read as when Congress passed it.

verdicts.claim: Under the mechanism, congress members voted only to put the question to students; a yes vote sent the fee to the Board of Regents, which held the final decision. Executive vice president John Bradley expected the board to decide at its 9 May 2003 quarterly meeting.
verdicts.note: wkuherald.com 403s a direct fetch; the article opens at Wayback capture 20210801054344. It carries all three: Bradley reminding members they were not voting for a fee but for an opportunity for students to voice an opinion; "If students vote for the proposal, if will passed on to the Board of Regents, who will make the final vote" (sic); and Bradley saying the board would probably decide at its next quarterly meeting May 9.

verdicts.claim: The $3 radio fee referendum passed 1,066 to 765 in an election in which 2,014 students voted; the result was announced by chief justice Holly Skidmore shortly after 1 a.m. on the Friday.
verdicts.note: Opened at Wayback capture 20220126073104. All four numbers and the Skidmore 1 a.m. detail are in the article. Headline capitalisation on the live site is "Martin, johnson win contested SGA election races"; the label matches.

verdicts.claim: The Board of Regents' quarterly meeting of 9 May 2003 carried "library, facility improvement and radio station fees" among its agenda items, per TopSCHOLAR's description of the minutes. The outcome of the radio station fee item is not established in the sources reachable for this pass.
verdicts.note: The TopSCHOLAR landing page opens and the description string is exact, with start date 9 May 2003. I confirmed the caveat independently: the minutes PDF (viewcontent.cgi?article=1753&context=bor) returned HTTP 202 with a zero-byte body on two paced attempts, so the outcome genuinely is not reachable. The fact states its own limit honestly, which is the right handling.

verdicts.claim: The new constitution and bylaws were carried as Bill 03-10-F, "New Constitution and Bylaws," dated 10 November 2003 in SGA's legislation archive. The Herald gave the first reading as 11 November 2003.
verdicts.fixed: The new constitution and bylaws were carried as Bill 03-10-F, "New Constitution and Bylaws," dated 10 November 2003 in SGA's legislation archive. No reachable source gives the date of its first reading.

I checked further: data/herald-index-full.json has no November or December 2003 item on the constitution (the run of Ashlee Clark SGA items resumes 5 February 2004), data/years.json holds no first-reading date for this bill, and B03-10-F.pdf is not in the Wayback record for that folder. The 11 November date has no support anywhere I can reach.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 constitution is headed "As Proposed Fall 2003" and names three branches: an Executive Cabinet of seven, the Student Senate, and the Judicial Council. The three elected offices were President, Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President; the Chief of Staff, Director of Public Relations, Director of Information Technology and Director of Academic and Student Affairs were appointed and all seven had a vote in the cabinet.
verdicts.fixed: The 2004 constitution is headed "As Proposed Fall 2003" and divides SGA into an executive, a legislative and a judicial branch; the executive branch is a seven-member Executive Cabinet, the legislative branch is the Student Senate and the judicial branch is the Judicial Council. The three elected offices were President, Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President; the Chief of Staff, Director of Public Relations, Director of Information Technology and Director of Academic and Student Affairs were appointed and all seven had a vote in the cabinet.
verdicts.note: Heading exact. Everything about the seven offices is right: 2.1, 2.6.1, 2.7.1, 2.8.1, 2.9.1, and votes at 2.3.16, 2.4.8, 2.5.13, 2.6.7, 2.7.11, 2.8.7, 2.9.7. But the cited clause 1.2 names "the executive branch, the legislative branch, and the judicial branch" and nothing more; the Executive Cabinet is constituted at 2.10, the Senate named at 3.1, the Judicial Council at 4.1. As written the fact puts words in clause 1.2 that are not there. Same effect, wrong attribution.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 constitution set the Senate at 35 seats: four representatives from each of the senior, junior, sophomore and freshman classes, two graduate students and seventeen at-large. All but the four freshman seats and three at-large seats were elected in the spring; unfilled graduate seats converted to at-large seats at the fall elections. Vacancies after the fall elections were filled by presidential appointment with a majority of the Senate.
verdicts.note: Clauses 3.6.1 to 3.6.7, 3.7.1, 3.7.2, 3.9.1. The document does not print the figure 35; it is the sum of 16 + 2 + 17, which is arithmetic on the listed seats and fair to state.

verdicts.claim: Under the 2004 constitution the Speaker of the Senate was elected from the elected Senate by the previous semester's legislative branch, served as Coordinator of Committees, and appointed the Secretary of the Senate subject to Senate approval. Committee chairs were appointed by the Speaker with a majority vote of the Senate.
verdicts.note: Clauses 3.2.4, 3.3.2, 3.4.1, and 5.3.6 through 5.7.4 (each of the five committees has its chair appointed by the Speaker with a majority of the Senate).

verdicts.claim: The 2004 constitution named five standing committees as part of the legislative branch: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements. It also created an Organizational-Aid Board of five members appointed by the President and approved by the Senate, a body absent from the Spring 2001 constitution.
verdicts.note: Clause 5.1 makes standing committees part of the legislative branch; 5.3 to 5.7 name the five. Section 6.1.1 gives the Organizational-Aid Board its five presidential appointees approved by the Senate. I checked the Spring 2001 text for any equivalent body and there is none, so the comparison holds.

verdicts.claim: The Executive Cabinet held a veto over all Senate legislation, carried by a majority of the cabinet, with written reasons to the sponsoring committee within forty-eight hours. The 2004 constitution set the override at three-fourths of the Senate while the 2004 bylaws set it at two-thirds of those present and voting, an inconsistency between the two documents.
verdicts.note: Constitution 2.10.4 (veto, majority of cabinet, 48 hours to the sponsoring committee) and 3.8.9 (three-fourths); bylaws Article VI section 3 item 6 ("A two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Senate, present and voting, can override"). The two documents do contradict each other, and both thresholds are quoted correctly. A real and worthwhile finding.

verdicts.claim: Impeachment of any executive officer, senator or justice required a written endorsement of at least twenty percent of the Senate's membership to initiate, a special session presided over by the Chief Justice (by the Speaker for justices), a final vote no sooner than fourteen days after proceedings began, and a two-thirds vote of the full Senate membership sitting as a judicial body.
verdicts.note: Clauses 2.12.1-4, 3.10.1-4 and 4.6.1-4. The parenthetical is right: 4.6.3 puts the Speaker in the chair for a justice's impeachment while 2.12.3 and 3.10.3 give it to the Chief Justice.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 bylaws set quorum at a simple majority of Senate members, allowed senators no more than four absences a semester unless excused by the Judicial Council, fixed Senate meetings at 5 p.m. every Tuesday, and required every senator except the Speaker and the University Senate representatives to serve on at least one committee.
verdicts.note: Bylaws Article V section 2 (quorum), Article III section 2 (four absences), Article IV section 1 (5:00 pm every Tuesday, Senate Chambers), Article VIII section 6 (committee service, Speaker and University Senate representatives excepted). Four for four.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 constitution put a five-justice Judicial Council, appointed by the President with a two-thirds vote of the Senate, in office no later than two weeks after the start of the fall term for one academic year. The council had to meet at least twice a month, adjudicate election appeals, and review all constitutional amendments before the Senate voted on them.
verdicts.note: Clauses 4.3.1, 4.3.2, 9.4 (one academic year), 4.5.11 (twice a month), 4.5.5 (election appeals), 4.5.9 (review amendments before the Senate's vote).

verdicts.claim: On a presidential vacancy the 2004 constitution gave the President's duties to the Executive Vice President but sent the Student Regent seat to a special election of the student body, as required by KRS 164.321, with the Judicial Council controlling the timeline, applications and campaigning. The Spring 2001 constitution had filled the whole office, regent seat included, by special election.
verdicts.note: Clauses 2.11.1, 2.11.2 (with the KRS 164.321 citation printed in the text) and 2.11.3; against Spring 2001 clause 2.9.1, which fills the position "including the duty of Student Regent" by special election. The contrast is real and is the constitutional basis for the split the archive already records in April 2004.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 constitution kept the amendment rule at two-thirds of the full Senate membership plus a referendum of a majority of students voting, but dropped the Spring 2001 clause subjecting all constitutional changes to the approval of the university administration.
verdicts.note: Section 10 of the 2004 text contains only clause 10.1, which matches Spring 2001 clause 9.1; there is no counterpart to 9.2 anywhere in the 2004 document. I read the whole section to confirm the absence rather than assume it.

verdicts.claim: The 2004 Election Codes, adopted 22 January 2004, gave the Judicial Council supervision of all elections, set filing between 1 February and 2 March, made a candidate orientation on 17 February compulsory on pain of disqualification, and capped spending at $450 for president, $400 for executive vice president, $350 for other executive offices and $50 for legislative candidates, with no single donor giving more than $100.
verdicts.note: The .doc opens and carries "Adopted 1-22-04," the Judicial Council authority line, the 1 February to 2 March filing window, the 17 February 7 p.m. orientation with disqualification for non-attendance, and all four spending caps plus the $100 donor limit. One small softening the fact omits: the orientation requirement carries an exemption clause ("unless an exemption by the Judicial Council has been granted"). Not enough to trim, but worth the editor knowing.

verdicts.claim: Students adopted a list of 40 amendments to the SGA constitution, compiled by the Legislative Research Committee, by 1,193 votes to 262 at the March 2005 general election. The Talisman fee question on the same ballot passed 1,019 to 669, and all 25 senate candidates were elected to 28 open seats.
verdicts.note: The Wayback capture of the 17 March 2005 Herald opens in full. It carries the 40-amendment referendum at 1,193 to 262, names the legislative research committee as compiler, gives the Talisman fee at 1,019 to 669, and says all 25 senators on the ballot filled some of 28 open seats. Every number checks.

verdicts.claim: The document SGA afterwards published as its constitution is headed "As Proposed Spring 2005." Against the 2004 text it raised the grade point average for a senate seat and for senate office from 2.0 to 2.5, lowered the veto override from three-fourths to two-thirds, moved appointment of committee chairs from the Speaker to the President, raised the Speaker's minimum office hours from five to eight a week, seated the Speaker on the Executive Cabinet as an ex-officio non-voting member, and required the Speaker to be at least a sophomore with a year's service as a senator.
verdicts.note: I diffed the two documents clause by clause. Senate office 3.2.1 and senate seat 3.5.1 both move 2.0 to 2.5; override 3.8.9 moves 3/4 to 2/3; committee chairs at 5.3.6, 5.4.4, 5.5.4, 5.6.6 and 5.7.4 all move from Speaker to President; Speaker's hours 3.3.7 move five to eight; new 3.3.8 seats the Speaker on the cabinet ex-officio non-voting; new 3.3.9 sets the sophomore and one-year-as-senator bar. Six for six. The fact is careful to say "the document SGA afterwards published," not that it is the 40-amendment package, which is the right restraint.

verdicts.claim: The Spring 2005 constitution added two removal procedures the 2004 document lacked: removal of a committee head, with the vice-chair acting until a replacement was appointed, and a vote of no confidence in the Speaker of the Senate, with the Legislative Research Committee head serving as interim Speaker. Both used the same twenty percent endorsement, fourteen-day and two-thirds thresholds as impeachment.
verdicts.note: New sections 3.11 (committee head removal, vice-chair acting) and 3.12 (vote of no confidence, LRC head as interim Speaker), neither present in the 2004 text. Thresholds at 3.11.2/3.11.4 and 3.12.2/3.12.4 match the impeachment thresholds exactly.

verdicts.claim: The Spring 2005 bylaws cut the permitted absences for a senator from four a semester to three, raised the number of student University Senate representatives reporting to the Senate from three to five, required authors to attend a Legislative Research Committee meeting and defend their legislation within two weeks, corrected the fiscal record-keeping reference from Bill 03-03-S to Bill 02-07-F, and set their own ratification for fall 2005.
verdicts.note: All five verified against the 2004 bylaws: three absences (Art III s2, was four), five University Senate representatives (Art V s1 item 7, was three), the new author-defence clause in Art VI, Bill 02-07-F in Art VII s4 (was 03-03-S), and Art XI s1 "implemented for the Fall 2005" (was Fall 2004). I also confirmed the block's own caveat: the file's first line still reads "As Proposed Fall 2003," so the heading is a drafting leftover, exactly as unanswered note 3 says.

verdicts.claim: The senate roster ran well below and then above the constitutional 35: eighteen seats with eight senators present on 5 September 2006, thirty-one seats with twenty-two present on 28 November 2006 and sixteen present on 5 December 2006.
verdicts.fixed: The senate roster ran below the constitutional 35 all year: eighteen seats with eight senators present on 5 September 2006, thirty-one seats with twenty-two present on 28 November 2006 and sixteen present on 5 December 2006.
verdicts.note: All four numbers are right, read from the mirrored PDFs at data/documents/2006-07-sga-minutes-05-sep-2006.pdf, -28-nov-2006.pdf and -05-dec-2006.pdf ("8 of 18 Senators present," "22 of 31," "16 of 31"). But 18 and 31 are both under 35, so "and then above" is contradicted by the fact's own figures. Two further points for the editor: the fact cites only Minutes/717 while resting on three separate meetings, and the 28 November minutes open with Robert Watkins formally resigning the presidency and Jeanne Johnson due to be sworn in on 5 December, which is why the December minutes head the Executive Vice-President line "Vacant."

verdicts.claim: SGA's senate minutes numbered the sessions: the meeting of 5 September 2006 is recorded as the first meeting of "the fifth Student Government Association," that of 28 November 2006 as the twelfth and that of 5 December 2006 as the thirteenth. The archive does not establish what year the numbering counts from.
verdicts.note: All three phrases verified in the mirrored PDFs: "The first meeting of the fifth Student Government Association... September 5, 2006," "The twelfth meeting of the fifth... November 28, 2006," "The thirteenth meeting of the fifth... December 5, 2006." The refusal to guess what the numbering counts from is correct and should stay.

rewritten:
The Student Government Association's governing documents in these years were the constitution and the Executive and Legislative Bylaws, joined from spring 2022 by the Judicial Council's General Procedural Rules, which that document ranks equal to the bylaws, and by the Election Codes the Judicial Council enacts under the constitution. The constitution set the three branches, the executive offices, the Senate's seats, the standing committees and the removal procedures, and provided that it be amended by a Senate vote and a subsequent student referendum. The archive holds no complete bylaws text before February 2026, so what the bylaws contained in the earlier years is known only through the bills that amended particular sections.

Resolution 5-13-S, written by Cory Dodds, then student body president, and sponsored by Legislative Research, had its first reading on 19 February 2013 and its second on 26 February. It adopted amendments to both the constitution and the bylaws and referred the constitutional changes to the student body for ratification on the spring 2013 ballot. The proposed changes cut each class delegation from four senators to three, gave each academic college one elected senator, cut at-large seats from seventeen to fifteen, seated the president of each regional affiliate in the Senate, extended Judicial Council terms from one year to the length of a justice's academic career, and reduced the Organizational Aid Board from ten members to six. The archive does not record the spring 2013 result. A referendum in the fall 2013 election created a Navitas and English as a Second Language international student seat: 426 of the 564 students who voted cast a ballot on it, and it passed with 310 yes votes, 73 per cent.

Committees entered the constitution one at a time. Bills 16-16-F and 17-16-F, given a second reading on 15 November 2016, made the Sustainability Committee permanent and made MyCampusToo permanent under the name the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion. Bill 27-17-S added the Committee Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm on 4 April 2017, passing 27-0-1. The same night Bill 21-17-S passed 24-7-0, cutting the membership grade point average floor in three clauses from 2.5 to 2.0. The Herald reported on 19 April 2017 that all six referendums on that spring's ballot passed. The text reissued as amended spring 2017 carried a 36-seat Senate, eight standing committees, and a seven-justice Judicial Council appointed by the president on a two-thirds Senate vote.

Bill 8-20-S, A Bill to Initiate Emergency Clauses, had its first reading on 14 April 2020, in response to the university's closure over COVID-19. It provided that officers and senators could extend their terms until an election could be held and that the president could extend the student regent position, and set the rescheduled spring 2020 election within three weeks of the start of the fall semester. Those provisions now stand as Section 11 of the constitution, where the deadline reads four weeks.

The text WKU posted for 2023-24 was a different document: seven standing committees under new names and thirty-seven Senate seats, among them transfer and non-traditional, First-Generation and International Student Engagement Center seats. Three bills from the Legislative Operations Committee, read on 7 and 14 November 2023, corrected the documents against themselves. Bill 8-23-F replaced University Senate with Faculty Senate, because that body had split into a Faculty Senate and a Staff Senate and SGA members were chartered only for the Faculty Senate. Bill 10-23-F brought committee names into line with names the Senate had already changed in Bill 4-22-F. Bill 9-23-F struck the bylaws sections on expelling senators, because the constitution provided for impeachment and made no mention of expulsion.

A package of constitutional amendment bills, each authored by four senators and three members of the Judicial Council and sponsored by the Legislative Operations Committee and the Judicial Council, had its second reading on 28 March 2024. Bill 20-24-S renamed the Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President as Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, and the Director of Public Relations as Chief Communications Officer. Bill 19-24-S struck the Director of Information Technology and the Director of Enrollment and Student Experience and moved their duties to the two vice presidencies. Bill 29-24-S raised the grade point average floors to 2.75 for executive officers and 2.5 for senators and justices. Bill 26-24-S required removal after a second censure in one academic year. Bill 32-24-S moved committee-head appointments from the president to the speaker. Bill 22-24-S changed the amendment rule from two-thirds of the full Senate to two-thirds of the senators present. The bill sheets record no vote counts, and no referendum on these amendments appears in the archive, though the changes are in the constitution WKU has posted since.

In the April 2025 election students ratified Bill 21-25-S, renaming the diversity committee the Action and Opportunity Committee, with 88 per cent in favour. The Senate adopted a codified rewrite of the Executive and Legislative Bylaws on 24 February 2026.
problems:
Eight problems, in rough order of seriousness.

1. Numbers and dates the facts do not carry. "On 19 April students ratified six amendments" and "88 per cent in favour" in "April 2025" appear in no entry in the structure array. Both are true and are already in data/years.json, sourced to the Herald of 19 April 2017 ("all six referendums were passed") and 16 April 2025, and I confirmed the 2017 one in an Internet Archive capture of the article. But a summary must not carry a count and a percentage that the fact list beneath it cannot support. Two facts need adding to the structure before this is published, or the figures come out.

2. "Two documents governed the Student Government Association through these years" is contradicted by the writer's own facts. Fact 18 records the Judicial Council's General Procedural Rules, adopted spring 2022, which their own text ranks equal to the Legislative Bylaws and which give the Council a veto over Senate legislation. Fact 37 records the Election Codes, enacted by the Judicial Council under clause 4.6.5. From 2022 there were four governing instruments, not two.

3. Continuity the archive does not hold. The first paragraph states what the bylaws set for the whole 2011 to 2026 span. The writer says plainly in the unanswered section that the archive holds no complete bylaws text before February 2026, and I confirmed that: data/documents and data/legislation/governing contain only the 2026 bylaws. What the bylaws contained before 2026 is known only through individual amendment bills, and the summary should say so rather than describe them as a settled thing.

4. A drafting body given a head it is not recorded as having. "A package of amendments drafted by a committee under Chief Justice Isaac King" is not what the bill sheets show. Bills 19, 20, 22, 26, 28, 29 and 32-24-S each list seven authors, headed by Meghan Pierce, Senator at Large, with King fifth of the seven, and are sponsored by the Legislative Operations Committee and the Judicial Council. Bill 19-24-S mentions a "Constitutional Referendum Committee" but names no chair. Making one of seven authors the head of the drafting committee is exactly the kind of promotion the house rules forbid.

5. "The Senate voted a package of amendments" on 28 March 2024. The bill sheets record a second reading on that date and leave the Pass and Fail lines blank. No vote count exists in the archive, and the writer notes in the unanswered section that no referendum on those amendments is recorded either, though the changes appear in the constitution WKU has posted since. The summary should say what the sheets say.

6. Res 5-13-S is described as having done what it only proposed. "It cut each class delegation from four senators to three... cut at-large seats from seventeen to fifteen" states these took effect, when the resolution adopted the amendments and referred them to the spring 2013 ballot, and the archive does not record that result. The at-large figure makes the point: the resolution set fifteen, and the next constitution in the archive, spring 2017, has fourteen.

7. A later document read back into an earlier one. The summary calls the 2023-24 seat an "Intercultural Student Engagement Center" seat. That document's clause 3.6.11 reads "International Student Engagement Center". "Intercultural" is the wording of the 2024-25 text.

8. Smaller: "could be changed only by a Senate vote followed by a student referendum" is what clause 11.1/10.1 says, but the summary states it as a fact about how the constitution actually changed, while the writer's own unanswered section shows that referendums are mostly unrecorded and the March 2024 changes reached the posted text with no referendum in evidence. The word "only" should go.

Two structure-level notes that do not by themselves force a rewrite: fact 23 misnumbers a clause and misstates which seats convert to at-large, and facts 6, 28, 30, 31, 32 and 33 each cover two bills but carry a single URL, so half the citations are unlinked.

claims_rejected.claim: Clause 3.2.2 of the 2023-24 constitution states that the Speaker has no voting powers in Senate meetings over which they preside except to break a tie. Clause 3.10.1 leaves vacancies after the fall elections to be filled by presidential appointment with majority Senate approval, and clause 3.9.6 turns unfilled graduate, Gatton Academy and academic-college seats into at-large positions in the same fall election.
claims_rejected.fixed: Clause 3.2.2 of the 2023-24 constitution states that the Speaker has no voting powers in Senate meetings over which they preside except to break a tie. Clause 3.10.1 leaves vacancies after the fall elections to be filled by presidential appointment with majority Senate approval, and clause 3.9.2 turns unfilled freshman, graduate, International and Gatton Academy seats into at-large positions in the same fall election.
claims_rejected.note: The first two parts check out. The third does not. Section 3.9 of the 2023-24 text has only two clauses; there is no 3.9.6. The rule is at 3.9.2, and it covers freshman, graduate, International and Gatton Academy seats, not academic-college seats. The wording given is the 2017 constitution's clause 3.7.6 (graduate, Gatton Academy and academic college), which appears to have been carried forward from the earlier document by mistake.

verdicts.claim: Resolution 5-13-S, first reading 19 February 2013 and second reading 26 February 2013, author Cory Dodds, sponsor Legislative Research, adopted amendments to both the constitution and the bylaws and referred the constitutional changes to the student body for ratification on the spring 2013 election ballot.
verdicts.note: Read the scanned resolution at data/legislation/2012-13/r5-13-s.pdf (page 1 rendered to image; the PDF carries no text layer). Cover sheet gives First Reading February 19, 2013, Second Reading February 26, 2013, AUTHOR Cory Dodds, SPONSOR Legislative Research, and a THEREFORE clause referring the amendments to the student body for ratification on the spring 2013 election ballot, plus a second THEREFORE adopting the bylaws amendments. The Pass line on the sheet is blank.

verdicts.claim: Under Resolution 5-13-S the number of senators for each class was reduced from four to three (clauses 3.6.1-3.6.4), students in each academic college elected one senator (3.6.7), at-large senators were reduced from seventeen to fifteen (3.6.8), and the president of each regional affiliate became a member of the Student Senate (3.6.9).
verdicts.note: Confirmed on the Overview of Major Changes sheet (page 3 of the same PDF), Article 3, bullet by bullet, with the same clause numbers.

verdicts.claim: Resolution 5-13-S changed the Judicial Council term of office from one year to the duration of a justice's academic career at WKU provided they maintained the requirements of office (clauses 4.3.4 and 10.4), and reduced Organizational Aid Board membership from ten to six (7.1.1).
verdicts.note: Overview of Major Changes, Article 4 first bullet (4.3.4/10.4) and Article 7 (7.1.1, reduced from ten to six 'to reflect current custom').

verdicts.claim: The fall 2013 referendum creating a Navitas and English as a Second Language international student senate seat drew 426 votes out of the 564 students who voted in the election, and passed with 310 yes votes, 73 per cent.
verdicts.note: wkuherald.com returns 403 to us now, so I read the article in the Internet Archive capture of 18 June 2021. Herald Staff, 19 September 2013, 'SGA election results in, new senate seat created': 564 voters, 426 votes cast on the referendum, 310 or 73 percent yes. All three figures match.

verdicts.claim: Bill 21-17-S, first reading 21 March 2017 and second reading 4 April 2017, passed 24-7-0 and amended sections 2.2.1, 3.2.1 and 4.2.3 of the constitution from a 2.5 cumulative grade point average requirement to 2.0.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2016-17/bill_21-17-s.pdf, whose source_url in data/legislation.json is the URL cited. Header gives both readings and 'Pass: YES; 24-7-0'; the first WHEREAS names sections 2.2.1, 3.2.1 and 4.2.3 and both GPA figures.

verdicts.claim: Bill 16-16-F and Bill 17-16-F, both given first reading 1 November 2016 and second reading 15 November 2016, added the Sustainability Committee and MyCampusToo, renamed the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion, to the constitution as permanent committees.
verdicts.note: Both bill sheets read locally (bill-16-16-f.pdf, bill_17-16-f.pdf); both carry those two reading dates and 'Pass: YES', and 17-16-F states MyCampusToo is listed 'as the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion'. One housekeeping point: the src_url resolves only to 16-16-F, so 17-16-F is cited without its own link.

verdicts.claim: Bill 27-17-S, second reading 4 April 2017, passed 27-0-1 and added the Committee Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm to the constitution as a permanent committee.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2016-17/bill_27-17-s.pdf: 'Pass: YES; 27-0-1' and the SAVES committee named in full. Worth noting the sheet records first reading on 4 April 2017 as well, so both readings fell on the same night.

verdicts.claim: The constitution as amended spring 2017 set the Senate at 36 seats: three senior, three junior, three sophomore and three freshman class senators, two graduate senators, one English as a Second Language international senator, one Gatton Academy senator, one senator from each of six academic colleges, and fourteen at-large senators.
verdicts.note: data/documents/2017-18-sga-constitution.pdf, clauses 3.6.1-3.6.9, matches item for item. The document does not print a total; 36 is the sum of the clauses the claim itself lists, which is a fair reading.

verdicts.claim: The spring 2017 constitution named eight standing committees: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations, Campus Improvements, Diversity and Inclusion, Sustainability, and SAVES. Committee heads were appointed by the President and approved by a majority of the Senate.
verdicts.note: Section 5 of the same file runs 5.2 to 5.9, eight committees in exactly that order, and 5.1.2 gives appointment by the President with approval by the majority of the Senate.

verdicts.claim: Under the spring 2017 constitution the Judicial Council was seven justices appointed by the President with the approval of a two-thirds vote of the Senate, taking office no later than two weeks after the beginning of the fall term and serving for the duration of their academic career.
verdicts.note: Clauses 4.3.1, 4.3.2 and 4.3.5 of the 2017 text, with 10.4 repeating the term of service.

verdicts.claim: Impeachment of an executive officer, senator or justice required a written endorsement of at least twenty per cent of Senate membership; proceedings were held in a special session of the Senate; a final vote could not be called until at least fourteen days after proceedings were initiated; and removal required a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate sitting as a judicial body.
verdicts.note: The three parallel sets 2.12.2-2.12.4, 3.9.2-3.9.4 and 4.7.2-4.7.4 all read as claimed. The claim sensibly does not assert who presides, which differs between the three.

verdicts.claim: Under the spring 2017 constitution, section 11.1, the constitution could be amended by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate and a subsequent referendum carried by a majority of the student body voting. That text was unchanged in the version posted for 2023-24, where it appears as section 10.1.
verdicts.note: 2017 clause 11.1 and 2023-24 clause 10.1 are word for word identical; I compared both files directly.

verdicts.claim: Bill 1-17-F, first reading 28 August 2017, added clauses 4.6.12 and 4.6.13 giving the Judicial Council the duty to establish a temporary committee of the Judicial Council and members of the Senate and Executive bodies for formulating constitutional amendments, and to update the constitution with amendments approved in student body referendums.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2017-18/bill-1-17-f.pdf gives First Reading August 28th, 2017 and quotes both new clauses in those words. The Second Reading and Pass lines are blank on the sheet, and the claim correctly stops at the first reading.

verdicts.claim: Bill 4-17-F, first reading 28 August 2017, added clause 3.2.5 requiring every senator to post a minimum of one set office hour per week.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2017-18/bill-4-17-f.pdf: first reading 28 August 2017; new Section 3.2.5 to read 'Be able to post a minimum of one (1) set office hour per week'. Second reading and pass lines blank.

verdicts.claim: Bill 8-20-S, A Bill to Initiate Emergency Clauses, had its first reading on 14 April 2020. Its authors were Dawson McCoun and MJ Mayo. It required a two-thirds majority vote of the Senate together with a majority vote of the Executive Cabinet and a majority vote of the Judicial Council to initiate the clauses, and set the rescheduled spring 2020 election to be held within three weeks of the start of the fall 2020 semester.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2019-20/8_20_s.pdf: First Reading 04/14/20; PURPOSE sets the three-body vote requirement; a WHEREAS sets the rescheduled spring 2020 election within three weeks of Fall 2020; AUTHORS Dawson McCoun, MJ Mayo.

verdicts.claim: As carried into the constitution as Section 11, the emergency provisions allow officers and senators to extend their terms until a new election can be held, allow Zoom or another virtual platform in place of in-person Senate meetings, allow the President to extend the student regent position, and set the rescheduled election within four weeks of the new semester, not the three weeks in the original bill.
verdicts.note: 2023-24 constitution clauses 11.2.1, 11.2.2, 11.2.4 and 11.2.3. The three-to-four week change is real and is correctly flagged rather than smoothed over.

verdicts.claim: Bill 17-22-S, first reading 1 March 2022 and second reading 8 March 2022, supported adoption of the General Procedural Rules of the Judicial Council. The bill stated that the Judicial Council had previously had no formal written established guidelines or procedures pertaining to its functions and duties.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2021-22/17_22_s.pdf: readings 3-1-22 and 3-8-22, and the first WHEREAS says exactly that. Pass line blank.

verdicts.claim: The Judicial Council's General Procedural Rules, as adopted spring 2022, rank the document as subordinate to the constitution and equal to the Legislative Bylaws, allow the Judicial Council to veto Senate legislation with a report to the author and the Speaker within fourteen days, and allow the Senate to override a Judicial Council veto by a two-thirds vote of those present and voting.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/governing/jc_general_procedures.pdf, section 1.1 (subordination and equality with the Legislative Bylaws), 1.2.1 (report to author within two weeks and to the Speaker) and 1.2.3 (two-thirds of the Senate present and voting).

verdicts.claim: Bill 16-22-S, first reading 1 March 2022 and second reading 8 March 2022, added a definition of good standing to clause 3.6.2: satisfying WKU's requirements for attendance and satisfactory progress toward completion of coursework, and a term GPA, WKU GPA and Overall Higher Education GPA of 2.0.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2021-22/16_22_s.pdf quotes the new 3.6.2 in those words, with both reading dates as claimed.

verdicts.claim: Bill 21-22-S, first reading 8 March 2022 and second reading 22 March 2022, amended the constitution to establish a Community Relations Committee responsible for advocating for students' needs in Bowling Green and coordinating volunteer service and a yearly voter drive.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2021-22/21_22_s.pdf: readings 3-8-22 and 3-22-22, and the WHEREAS clauses cover Bowling Green advocacy, volunteer service and 'coordinating yearly voter drive'.

verdicts.claim: The constitution posted by WKU for 2023-24 set the Senate at thirty-seven seats: twelve class senators, one graduate, one international, one Gatton Academy, one senator from each of five academic colleges, fourteen at-large, one transfer/non-traditional, one International Student Engagement Center and one First-Generation senator.
verdicts.note: Clauses 3.6.1-3.6.12 of data/documents/2023-24-sga-constitution.pdf sum to 37 and the seat types match, including 3.6.11 reading 'International Student Engagement Center', which is what that document says.

verdicts.claim: The 2023-24 constitution named seven standing committees: Legislative Operations, Enrollment and Student Experience, Outreach and Student Experience, Campus Improvements and Sustainability, Diversity Equity and Inclusion, Student Mental Health and Wellbeing, and Community Relations. Committee heads were appointed by the President and approved by two-thirds of the Senate.
verdicts.note: Clauses 3.8.2 through 3.8.8 give those seven committees in that order, and 3.8.1.2 gives appointment by the President with approval by two-thirds of the Senate.

verdicts.claim: Clause 3.2.2 of the 2023-24 constitution states that the Speaker has no voting powers in Senate meetings over which they preside except to break a tie. Clause 3.10.1 leaves vacancies after the fall elections to be filled by presidential appointment with majority Senate approval, and clause 3.9.6 turns unfilled graduate, Gatton Academy and academic-college seats into at-large positions in the same fall election.
verdicts.fixed: Clause 3.2.2 of the 2023-24 constitution states that the Speaker has no voting powers in Senate meetings over which they preside except to break a tie. Clause 3.10.1 leaves vacancies after the fall elections to be filled by presidential appointment with majority Senate approval, and clause 3.9.2 turns unfilled freshman, graduate, International and Gatton Academy seats into at-large positions in the same fall election.
verdicts.note: The first two parts check out. The third does not. Section 3.9 of the 2023-24 text has only two clauses; there is no 3.9.6. The rule is at 3.9.2, and it covers freshman, graduate, International and Gatton Academy seats, not academic-college seats. The wording given is the 2017 constitution's clause 3.7.6 (graduate, Gatton Academy and academic college), which appears to have been carried forward from the earlier document by mistake.

verdicts.claim: The 2023-24 constitution set out a Judicial Appeal Process at clause 4.6.2: an appeal must meet one of three criteria (new facts, procedural issues, or a petition signed by no fewer than ten students), be filed within thirty days of the original ruling, be heard within five class days of receipt with at least 48 hours notice, and twelve hours notice where election rules are at issue; after 31 days the decision is final.
verdicts.note: Clauses 4.6.2.1 (three criteria, petition of no less than ten students), 4.6.2.2 (30 days), 4.6.2.3.1 (five class days, 48 hours, 12 hours for election matters) and 4.6.2.5 (final after 31 days). Every element checks.

verdicts.claim: Bill 8-23-F, first reading 7 November 2023 and second reading 14 November 2023, amended clause 2.4.10 to replace University Senate appointments with Faculty Senate appointments, on the ground that the University Senate had since split into a Faculty Senate and a Staff Senate and SGA members were chartered to serve only on the Faculty Senate.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2023-24/bill_8_23_f.pdf: readings 11/7/23 and 11/14/23, clause 2.4.10 quoted before and after, and WHEREAS (2) and (3) give exactly that reasoning.

verdicts.claim: Bill 9-23-F, first reading 7 November 2023 and second reading 14 November 2023, retitled Section 6 of the bylaws, deleted clause 6.1.2 and Section 6.3 on expulsion from the Senate, and renumbered what followed, because the constitution described impeachment proceedings for a senator with no mention of expulsion and the bylaws are subordinate to the constitution.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2023-24/bill_9_23_f.pdf: retitles Section 6, removes 6.1.2 and 6.3 with subsequent subsections renumbered, and gives both stated grounds (constitution section 3.10 describes impeachment with no expulsion; bylaws subordinate to constitution).

verdicts.claim: Bill 10-23-F, first reading 7 November 2023 and second reading 14 November 2023, corrected clauses 2.4.6 and 2.9.6 to use the committee names the Senate had already adopted in Bill 4-22-F, replacing Committee of Enrollment and Student Experience with Enrollment and Student Experience Committee.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2023-24/bill_10_23_f.pdf, both clauses quoted before and after, with Bill 4-22-F named as the measure that made the rename.

verdicts.claim: Bill 12-23-F raised the Chief Justice's required office hours from one to five per week, and Bill 15-23-F added clause 4.6.9 requiring Judicial Council members to maintain two office hours monthly. Both had first reading 14 November 2023 and second reading 28 November 2023 and were authored by Chief Justice Isaac King.
verdicts.note: Both sheets read locally: 12-23-F amends 4.4.8 from one to five hours; 15-23-F inserts 4.6.9 'Maintain two (2) office hours monthly'; both dated 11/14/23 and 11/28/23; AUTHORS on both is Isaac King, Chief Justice.

verdicts.claim: Bill 13-23-F, first reading 14 November 2023 and second reading 28 November 2023, amended clause 3.6.8 to add the Mahurin Honors College to the academic colleges electing a senator, taking the college seats from five to six. It was authored by Associate Chief Justice Ellen Henderson and Mahurin Honors College student Audrey Clark and sponsored by the Judicial Council.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/2023-24/bill_13_23_f.pdf quotes 3.6.8 before ('a total of five (5)') and after ('including the Mahurin Honors College... a total of six (6)'), with both authors and the Judicial Council as sponsor.

verdicts.claim: Bill 20-24-S retitled the Executive Vice President as Vice President, the Administrative Vice President as Chief Financial Officer and the Director of Public Relations as Chief Communications Officer. Bill 19-24-S struck sections 2.8 and 2.9, abolishing the Director of Information Technology and the Director of Enrollment and Student Experience and transferring their duties to the two vice presidencies. Both had first reading 12 March 2024 and second reading 28 March 2024.
verdicts.note: Both sheets read locally, dates 3/12/24 and 3/28/24 on each. 20-24-S lists all three retitlings and the sections affected; 19-24-S strikes sections 2.8 and 2.9 and redistributes the duties. The bill is internally inconsistent about which vice presidency takes which set of duties, so the claim's neutral 'to the two vice presidencies' is the right level of precision.

verdicts.claim: Bill 29-24-S raised the grade point average floor in clause 2.2.1 from 2.0 to 2.75 for executive officers and in clause 3.5.1 from 2.0 to 2.5 for senators. Bill 26-24-S added clause 4.6.12, requiring the Judicial Council to remove members censured twice in the same academic year. Both had second reading 28 March 2024.
verdicts.note: Both sheets confirm, with second reading 3/28/24 on each. For completeness, 29-24-S also raised clause 4.2.3 (Judicial Council) to 2.5 and the good-standing GPA in 3.5.2 to 2.5; the claim omits those but does not misstate anything.

verdicts.claim: Bill 32-24-S moved the appointment of committee heads in clause 3.8.1.2 from the President to the Speaker of the Senate, still subject to approval by two-thirds of the Senate. Bill 28-24-S added section 8.2, requiring every executive budget expenditure to be documented on paper signed by the President, Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, with a copy to the SGA advisor.
verdicts.fixed: Bill 32-24-S moved the appointment of committee heads in clause 3.8.1.2 from the President to the Speaker of the Senate, still subject to approval by two-thirds of the Senate. Bill 28-24-S added section 8.2, requiring every executive budget expenditure to be documented on paper signed by the President, Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President, with a copy to the SGA advisor under clause 8.2.1. Those two titles were changed to Vice President and Chief Financial Officer by Bill 20-24-S, read the same night, and section 8.2 as now posted carries the new titles.
verdicts.note: The Bill 32-24-S half is exact. The Bill 28-24-S half puts words in the bill it does not use: its text names the 'President, Executive Vice President, and Administrative Vice President'. The renamed titles come from Bill 20-24-S, and they appear in section 8.2 only in the constitution posted afterwards, which I checked. Small, but it is a later document read back into an earlier one.

verdicts.claim: Bill 22-24-S changed clause 10.1 from amendment by a two-thirds vote of the full membership of the Senate to a two-thirds vote of the present senators. Bill 23-24-S changed clause 10.2.1 so that constitutional amendment elections are held during the fall and spring senator elections rather than at the end of the fall and spring semesters, on the stated ground that turnout is significantly higher in representative elections.
verdicts.note: Both sheets quote the old and new text of 10.1 and 10.2.1, and 23-24-S's WHEREAS (3) says voter turnout is significantly higher during elections for student body representatives. Both dated 3/12/24 and 3/28/24.

verdicts.claim: The constitution WKU posted after the April 2025 referendum lists five executive offices, President, Vice President and Chief Financial Officer plus a Chief of Staff and Chief Communications Officer, and seven committees, the sixth of which is the Action & Opportunity Committee. Clause 3.6.8 as printed reads "a total of five (6) senators" for the academic colleges, carrying both the old and the new count.
verdicts.fixed: The constitution WKU currently posts lists five executive offices at clause 2.1, President, Vice President and Chief Financial Officer plus a Chief of Staff and Chief Communications Officer, and seven standing committees, of which the fifth, at clause 3.8.6, is the Action & Opportunity Committee. Clause 3.6.8 as printed reads "a total of five (6) senators" for the academic colleges, carrying both the old and the new count.
verdicts.note: Clause 2.1 and the mis-set clause 3.6.8 are exact, and the 3.6.8 catch is a good one. Two problems. The committees run 3.8.2 to 3.8.8, so Action & Opportunity is the fifth of the seven, not the sixth; the writer appears to have read the clause number 3.8.6 as an ordinal. And the file carries no date, no reference to Bill 21-25-S and no mention of a referendum, so 'posted after the April 2025 referendum' is an identification made from elsewhere in the archive, not something this source states. The identification looks right (this text also renames the DEI committee), but it should not be presented as read off the document.

verdicts.claim: The Executive and Legislative Bylaws approved 24 February 2026 set quorum at a simple majority of Senate members minus the number of vacancies (clause 4.2.1), allow no more than two unexcused Senate absences per semester with the Speaker sending a member to the Judicial Council on the second (clause 2.1.3), and allow amendment of the bylaws by a two-thirds vote of senators present and voting after a first reading at the previous meeting (clause 1.3.1).
verdicts.note: data/legislation/governing/sga_bylaws_2026.pdf, title page dated 24 February 2026. Clauses 4.2.1, 2.1.3 and 1.3.1 all read as claimed, including the Speaker referring the member to the Judicial Council on the second unexcused absence.

verdicts.claim: The February 2026 bylaws state that they are subordinate to the constitution and to university rules and state law, that Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised, 12th Edition governs any matter they do not cover, and that they supersede all prior versions.
verdicts.note: Clause 1.1.1 gives the subordination and 1.1.2 the Robert's Rules point, both as claimed. The supersession language is in the enacting sentence on page 2 rather than in 1.1.1-1.1.2, so the source label is a shade off, but nothing in the claim is wrong.

verdicts.claim: The Election Codes for spring 2026, edited and approved by the Judicial Council on 23 February 2026 under constitutional clause 4.6.5, capped candidate spending at $500 for president, $250 for vice president, $250 for chief financial officer and $75 for senate candidates.
verdicts.note: data/legislation/governing/election_codes_spring_2026.pdf: 'Edited and approved by the Judicial Council on February 23rd, 2026'; clause 1.1 cites Section 4.6.5; clauses 4.1.1 to 4.1.4 give $500, $250, $250 and $75, repeated in the summary table.
